articles.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
paragraphs: Pedro Sánchez accused his opponents of hurling insults and lies but his conservative rival has promised a new era of politics
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo's PP holds a narrow lead in the opinion polls

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.

articles.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
paragraphs: Watch: Zelensky questions "strange" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

articles.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
paragraphs: Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.
Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion

articles.title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
paragraphs: How New York reacted to postponement of Macy's parade

Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.
"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.
Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.
Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.
On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.
The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

articles.title: Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
paragraphs: The French president said he was proud to have led efforts to ban Brazilian meat products
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron calling Brazilian meat "doped".

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry, which took effect in September.
The Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.
Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at the Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.

articles.title: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
paragraphs: Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.
Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

articles.title: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
paragraphs: FILE - Actor Gerard Depardieu arrives to face trial for the alleged sexual assaults of two women on a film set in 2021, on March 24, 2025 in Paris. Aurelien Morissard/AP hide caption

PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.
The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.

articles.title: As UN Secretary General's last day approaches, search for his replacement continues
paragraphs: The UN Secretary General's term ends this year, but the big powers at the UN have been unable to agree on a replacement. UN watchers worry that there will be little time to get up to speed.

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: It's crunch time for the U.N., as it looks to appoint its next secretary-general. Antonio Guterres is due to step down next month. But after nine rounds of straw polls in the Security Council, there's still no consensus on a successor. Here's NPR's Michele Kelemen.MICHELE KELEMEN, BYLINE: The Trump administration has been tight-lipped about its preferences for a new secretary-general and had been holding out hope for new candidates to jump in the race. But time is running out, says former U.S. Ambassador Robert Wood.ROBERT WOOD: I think it's too late, and I'm not sure anybody would want to enter the race at this particular point.KELEMEN: He says there's too much at stake.WOOD: Given the turmoil that we have in the world, all these raging wars, the bad need for the U.N. to be reformed, confidence in the U.N. at an all-time low, we need to get this decision right. It has to be the right person.KELEMEN: Wood sees this mostly as a race between two candidates - Rebeca Grynspan, a former vice president of Costa Rica who's led the U.N.'s Trade and Development Organization, and Italian Argentinian Rafael Grossi, who heads the U.N.'s nuclear watchdog. Guyana's former foreign minister and U.N. ambassador, Carolyn Rodrigues-Burkett, is also in the mix. A former ambassador from the United Arab Emirates, Lana Nusseibeh, is, too, though she's facing opposition from activists because of her country's support for a militia carrying out atrocities in Sudan. Latin American countries also say that this is their region's turn to lead the U.N., according to U.N. traditions of regional rotations.ELIZABETH COUSENS: It's a confounding process at this point because it is a very strong field.KELEMEN: That's Elizabeth Cousens, president of the U.N. Foundation, which advocates for a strong U.S. presence at the U.N. In the straw polls, all four of these top candidates have faced opposition from two or more permanent Security Council members. Cousens says it's time for the council to rally behind someone to get the candidate to the General Assembly floor before the year is up.COUSENS: It's a group of really capable people who've led institutions. They've reformed institutions. They've led negotiations. They've been in the front line of major geopolitical files. I mean, this is a serious group of people running for this role, and I do think it's important to give the field credit for that.KELEMEN: Another U.N. watcher, Anjali Dayal, who teaches international politics at Fordham University, says whoever emerges will have little time to get up to speed at a complicated time in world affairs.ANJALI DAYAL: We would never think that a private organization appointing someone in December to pick up the reins in January would be a good idea. We would not imagine that we would give them that little lead time to take over the stewardship of a massive, complicated organization - to staff up, to be briefed, to hit the ground running.KELEMEN: The State Department says it wants a secretary-general to get back to basics, working on peace and security rather than, quote, "the absurd, politicized, woke ideology that has undermined" the U.N.'s effectiveness. Dayal points out that the Trump administration did not go through the U.N. to launch a war against Iran, and Russia violated the U.N. Charter by invading Ukraine.DAYAL: And so being able to get this position involves satisfying permanent members that want to violate the terms of the Charter while committing to upholding the terms of the Charter - to hold the job, to perform it well for everybody else. So it's a tricky proposition, and that's why it's taking so long.KELEMEN: Behind the scenes, U.N. experts say there's probably some horse trading going on that could include promises of top U.N. jobs to permanent Security Council members to overcome veto threats.Michele Kelemen, NPR News, the State Department.

articles.title: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
paragraphs: FILE - Strobe Talbott, President Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin, July 16, 2008. Franka Bruns/AP hide caption
Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.
FILE - President-elect Bill Clinton and Strobe Talbott of Time magazine talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., Jan. 2, 1993. James Finley/AP hide caption
Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.

articles.title: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
paragraphs: Relatives and healthcare workers prepare to bury a victim of Ebola, in Beni, North Kivu province, Congo, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP hide caption

BUNIA, Congo — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

articles.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
paragraphs: In this photo provided by the North Korean government, leader Kim Jong Un inspects a facility the government says is for producing weapons-grade nuclear material at an undisclosed location in North Korea, Monday, Nov. 25, 2026. Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP hide caption

SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.
Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.
KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

articles.title: 'We have no interest in hearing from Huw Edwards', Downing Street says
paragraphs: The prime minister's spokesperson has said broadcasters must "act responsibly" and that "we have no interest in hearing" what Huw Edwards has to say, following a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.
Edwards, who was convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children, has been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary plus a podcast by the Observer and Tortoise Media.
"Our thoughts first and foremost will be with the victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We have no interest in hearing what he has to say," a Downing Street spokesperson said.
"There are extremely serious crimes and anyone convicted of them must face the consequences of their actions."
The No 10 spokesperson added that broadcasters "are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regards to their audiences when making decisions".

Pressed on whether the prime minister believed Channel 4 had not acted responsibly, they said: "Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them."

During the court case, Edwards admitted three counts of making indecent images of children. That involved having 41 images and videos, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.
Earlier, Environment Minister Emma Hardy said the plan by Channel 4 made her feel "sick", telling LBC, external it was giving a platform to "someone who is on the Sex Offenders Register".

articles.title: Dec Donnelly says I'm a Celebrity tension 'became much bigger deal than it should have'
paragraphs: Ant McPartlin and Dec Donnelly present the show and host their own podcast
I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here host Declan Donnelly has said tensions between Mariella Frostrup and AJ Odudu over cooking duties on the show "became a much bigger deal than it should have".

Co-host Ant McPartlin said "cooking makes things very tense in camp", adding: "If they could zoom out a little bit in there, they'll realise it's not that deep. But they just can't, once they're in there".

Donnelly and McPartlin discussed on their podcast how relations became fractious, when Odudu attempted to help Frostrup cook on Saturday's episode - the next day Odudu was distressed after Frostrup accused her of being "aggressive".
On Wednesday 887 people complained to Ofcom about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu.
Wayne Rooney tried to repair relations between AJ Odudu (left) and Mariella Frostrup on Sunday

Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation on Tuesday, and Odudu accepted, explaining it was "triggering" because "it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".
On their podcast, Hanging Out with Ant and Dec, Donnelly said tensions in camp started "surprisingly early".

articles.title: Five Gladiators will not return for new BBC series
paragraphs: Athena, real name Karenjeet Kaur Bains, is among the Gladiators who will not be returning for the new series
Five Gladiators stars will not be returning to the BBC television show for its upcoming series, it is understood.
Athena, Comet, Bionic, Phantom and Cyclone will not be featured when the show returns in 2027.
A spokesperson for the production said the departing cast members "remain part of the wider Gladiators family" and are taking part in the ongoing arena tour, which comes to an end in December.
Gladiators relaunched on the BBC in 2024, having originally been aired on ITV from 1992 until 2000, and then on Sky between 2008 and 2009.
A spokesperson for Gladiators said: "We would like to thank our incredible Superhuman athletes for their contribution to the success and power of the Gladiators TV show.
"While they will not be appearing in Series 4, they remain part of the wider Gladiators family, and you can currently see them across the remaining shows in the UK Gladiator Arena Tour 2026."
Athena, real name Karenjeet Kaur Bains, 30, is a powerlifter and former track and field athlete, while Comet, real name, Ella-Mae Rayner, 31, is a former elite-level gymnast.

articles.title: GTA 6 crashes into top end of music chart after its record launch
paragraphs: Ten songs from Grand Theft Auto 6 appear in the UK's Official Singles Chart top 100
Grand Theft Auto 6 has been swerving into online feeds and cultural conversations since its record-breaking launch last week.
But one area where the game is really making a dent is the world of music.

Flower In A Hurricane, the single from the game's official soundtrack album by Justice featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, has climbed to number three on the UK's Official Singles Chart.
Go Easy, a new track from Dua Lipa specially recorded for the game, is the highest new entry at 21.
Seven other songs recorded for GTA 6 by artists including Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen also placed in the top 100.
Video game music has topped the UK chart before, when Robbie Williams' It's Only Us, recorded for the FIFA 2000 soundtrack, got to number one.
Run Away With Me, a 2015 song by Carly Rae Jepsen used during a "needle drop" moment in the game's first chapter, has also seen a huge spike in listeners.

articles.title: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
paragraphs: Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music
Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.
Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.

Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".

Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.
Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off
He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.

Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

articles.title: The little Welsh town that transformed a Strictly star's career
paragraphs: Layton Williams and Nikita Kuzmin competed together on BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2023, where they finished as joint runners-up
Strictly Come Dancing star Layton Williams has credited living and working in a small Welsh town with transforming his career.
The Bad Education actor spent months in Mold, Flintshire, rehearsing for the role of Angel in the musical Rent, which he said marked a turning point in his career.
"I've got to be honest, before I lived in Mold, I had not a clue that Mold was a place that existed, but I completely fell in love with it," he said.
Williams, from Bury in Greater Manchester, feels so connected to the town that he insisted on having a show at the Theatr Clwyd on his upcoming tour, Layton Live.
"The producers were like, 'we've never had a specific request to go to Mold, but we will make it happen'. And I said 'Thank you'," Williams said in an interview with Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales.
The show marks the 20th anniversary of his stage debut and is a "whistle-stop musical tour" through his career, which includes musicals such as Everybody's Talking About Jamie and Cabaret.
Olivier Award-winning Williams began acting professionally in theatre aged 12, but it was in Mold where he had his first major theatre role as an adult and his unlikely love for the town began.

articles.title: ‘Percy Jackson and the Olympians’ Star Leah Sava Jeffries on Her Idea for Annabeth’s Gray Contacts and the Big Fan Surprise Coming in the Season 3 Finale: A ‘Dream Came True’
paragraphs: SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from “I Learn How to Grow Zombies,” Season 3, Episode 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians,” now streaming on Disney+.

Seventeen-year-old Leah Sava Jeffries carries the weight of the world on her shoulders in Season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” — literally. The story of Atlas, a Titan burdened by the unbearable task of holding up the sky, is one of the many Greek myths that serves as the basis for a Season 3 storyline. Related Stories Jessy Moussallem’s 'Faux Bijoux,' Laila Abbas’ 'America Is Behind the Door' Take Top Prizes at Marrakech's Atlas Workshops ‘A Girl Unknown,’ ‘Crawling Into Myself,’ ‘Concrete Land’ Take Main Prizes at Doha Film Festival

The Season 3 premiere saw Jeffries’ Annabeth kidnapped by a human-lion-scorpion hybrid monster called a manticore and taken across the country from Percy (Walker Scobell) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri). Annabeth faces her own struggles while her friends work to rescue her, which is new for the show; the first two seasons followed the trio going on epic quests together. With Annabeth separated for much of “The Titan’s Curse” — the third book in Rick Riordan’s “Percy Jackson” series, which Season 3 is based on — Jeffries’ main scene partners now are Charlie Bushnell, who plays Luke, and Dafne Keen, who plays Artemis.

That’s not the only way Season 3 is wading into uncharted waters. The first-ever screen interpretation of “Percy Jackson” was a pair of movies in the early 2010s based on Riordan’s first and second books. But Jeffries is keenly aware of the fact that “The Titan’s Curse” has never been adapted.

“It’s the first time anyone has ever seen it live action instead of just reading it in the book,” she says. “I want to make sure that I’m still delivering how the description was as much as I can, but then also still giving my own little twist with it.”While dedicated readers of the “Percy Jackson” books love to see Easter eggs in the TV show, Jeffries never wants the show to be for those fans alone. She points out many viewers hadn’t read the books until Seasons 1 and 2 came out and aims to perform for that audience too — especially as someone who hadn’t even been born yet when the original novel was released in 2005, she points out.

“Coming into these roles in the beginning was a tough thing because [the books] had such a big fan base already, and so many people that already knew about them before me,” Jeffries says. “It was a lot to learn from, but I’m so excited that I was able to get this role and embody the character as much as I can.”

Jeffries says she has learned a lot from Bushnell, 22, whom she acted opposite in several key scenes in Episodes 2 and 3 this season. She recalls him checking in after fight scenes or making sure he didn’t accidentally hit her during a take.

“He’s such a role model for people. I learned so much stuff from him. He’s just such a great person to work with as well as a scene partner,” Jeffries says. “You could just tell he loves doing what he does, and that’s such a big thing to see because even before the show has come out, with criticism, sometimes I still get in my head. But when I watch him working, his confidence and the way he goes about things, it just makes me have a brighter day, so I’m very grateful to work with him.”

articles.title: ‘The Hunting Wives’ Stars and Creator Break Down Margo and Sophie’s Dangerous Love Affair in Season 2: ‘It’s a F—-ed Up Commitment’ to ‘Move Past’ Murder
paragraphs: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Season 2 of “The Hunting Wives,” now streaming on Netflix.

Earlier this month, Texas shocked the nation by electing Democrats to the governorship, the U.S. Senate and several more key positions during this year’s midterm elections. But the Lone Star State’s politics have always been seen as dynamic and complicated to those in the know — like fans of “The Hunting Wives,” Netflix’s juicy, campy drama series about a group of wealthy, gun-loving and sexually fluid women from East Texas.

“I love our show, because you see both sides of this coin, and we’re making fun of each side,” says “The Hunting Wives” star Brittany Snow about the series’ depiction of Texas politics. Co-star Malin Åkerman adds, “We’re not going to say that we had anything to do with it, but there’s all these different people saying, ‘The Hunting Wives’ had something to do with Texas going blue!’ It’s a fun little moment for us right now.”

Åkerman plays Margo Banks, the housewives’ confident ringleader whose Republican husband Jed (Dermot Mulroney) is a favorite to become governor. But, in Season 1, her beautiful house of cards is torn apart with the arrival of Sophie (Snow), an East Coast liberal who is shocked by the dirty underbelly of her new Southern home. Margo is full of secrets that she’s intent on keeping from Sophie, and thinks she’s in the clear when the two begin falling in love (and deep, deep lust). But Season 1 ended with Sophie discovering that Margo had gotten pregnant by a teenager, Brad (George Ferrier), before having an abortion and murdering Brad’s girlfriend, Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe), for uncovering the truth. The only saving grace for Margo is that Sophie can’t do anything with the information, because when her brother, Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), attempts to intimidate Sophie on Margo’s behalf, Sophie hits him with her car and kills him instantly. Now, they’re both in trouble.

Because Sophie hid Kyle’s body and told no one what she did, Season 2 begins with Margo trying to get back into her good graces. Unaware that Kyle is even dead, she keeps calling his number, getting no response until a panicked Sophie uses AI to deepfake Kyle’s voice and keep the illusion up. In person, Sophie tries her best to avoid Margo, but she can’t control herself. So she uses Kyle’s voice to ask Margo whether any of their relationship was genuine. When Margo answers that it was “100% real,” not just a ploy to cover-up the murder, Sophie is finally ready to get back together. She meets Margo at the Banks’ lake house, where they have sex — which is rudely interrupted by Zelda (Dale Dickey), a woman from Margo’s past, who sneaks up and holds a gun point-blank to Margo’s head.

Zelda is the leader of a biker gang in Alba, Margo’s hometown. She suspects Kyle of impregnating and murdering her underage granddaughter, Ellie (Chloe Guidry), and is attacking Margo to get information about Kyle’s whereabouts. Zelda and the gang don’t believe Margo when she says she has no idea where he is until Sophie blurts out that Kyle couldn’t have killed Ellie because she killed him. Zelda pieces together that it was someone in the gang (Cam Gigandet as Gentle John) and shoots him in the head. Soon, the police show up and the gang gets shot to death. Margo and Sophie are escorted home before they can discuss what happened, and Sophie panics, worrying that Margo will tell the police what happened to Kyle. But she doesn’t. After ignoring several calls from Sophie, Margo shows up at Sophie’s apartment and forgives her — they’re even, since Margo is a murderer too. Related Stories Matt Damon Narrates Ford Racing's 'Go Like Hell' Thanksgiving Day Ad Directed by Zack Snyder India Targets at Least 10 Million AI Workers Through National AI Talent Mission, WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Hears

The two begin secretly dating again, but Jed and his staff keep Margo on a tight leash during his campaign for governor. So Sophie hatches up a plan: If Margo publicly admits that she’s had an abortion, she’ll be able to tank Jed’s campaign and leave him for Sophie while drumming up enough support and attention to maintain her wealthy lifestyle. But right before the couple is set to make a TV appearance, Jed tells Margo that he knows she killed Abby and that Sophie killed Kyle, and that she needs to be a “dutiful wife” if she wants to keep herself and her girlfriend out of prison. Margo does still confess to cheating on Jed and having an abortion on live TV, but instead of advocating for women’s rights, she calls herself a murderer and says that prayer has allowed her to find redemption. The move is received positively by Jed’s rightwing base, and Sophie freaks out. That night, she confronts Margo, who explains to Sophie that she did it to protect her and that they can never speak again. Sophie is enraged, and says that she’ll release her recording of Margo confessing to Abby’s murder unless Margo gives her $10 million. In a brief epilogue set two years later, Sophie is uber-rich but estranged from Margo. She receives a phone call from a mysterious number and only hears panicked breathing on the other end; it’s Margo, who is covered in blood.
Snow and Åkerman, in one interview, and series creator Rebecca Cutter, in a separate conversation, spoke to Variety about the absolute insanity playing out in their East Texan world.

articles.title: Gayle King’s Son-in-Law Virgil Miller Dies at 45
paragraphs: King to take a leave of absence from 'CBS Mornings'
Gayle King‘s son-in-law Virgil Miller has died at 45 following a battle with cancer.

“CBS Mornings” executive producer Jon Tower delivered the sad news to the morning show’s staff on Friday in a memo obtained by Variety. In the note, Tower shared that Miller died “over the Thanksgiving holiday” following a “courageous battle with cancer.”

Further details about Miller’s illness were not disclosed. King will take a week off from “CBS Mornings” to “help with family matters,” Tower wrote, as private arrangements are being made. The TV anchor is expected to return the week of Dec. 7. Related Stories ‘A Girl Unknown,’ ‘Crawling Into Myself,’ ‘Concrete Land’ Take Main Prizes at Doha Film Festival 'Ramayana' Doubled Visitors at Kerala's Jatayu Rock, Official Says as India Pitches Itself to Global Productions at WAVES Film Bazaar

“Our thoughts right now are with her daughter, and their two beautiful children,” Tower’s memo continues. “We’re respecting the family and giving them privacy as they get through this difficult time.”

In December 2020, Miller married King’s daughter, Kirby Bumpus, in a private ceremony at King’s best friend Oprah Winfrey’s Santa Barbara home. Miller and Bumpus shared two children, son Luca, 5, and daughter Grayson, 2. King is the mother of two children, Kirby Bumpus and son William Bumpus Jr., from her marriage to ex-husband William Bumpus.

Miller is a Florida A&M University alumnus. There, he earned a bachelor’s degree in biology and a master’s degree in public health, while becoming a prominent student leader and drum major of FAMU’s famed Marching 100.

King regularly shares glimpses of her family life on social media, often featuring her children, their spouses and her grandchildren as they celebrate birthdays and special occasions. On Father’s Day, King posted a cute candid shot of Virgil Miller, Kirby Bumpus, William Jr., and his wife, Elise, at a World Cup game in Los Angeles after she gifted them tickets for the holiday. King regularly referred to Miller as her “fav son-in-law” in those heartfelt posts.

articles.title: BAFTA 2027 Entries Revealed: 126 Best Film Contenders, 728 Performances and No Spot for ‘You Can See Everything’ Star Amanda Seyfried
paragraphs: That’s how many titles appear on BAFTA‘s draft Entered Films List for the 2027 EE BAFTA Film Awards, with submissions across every category open to them: best film, director, screenplay and all nine craft races, right down to special visual effects.

There are 126 best film entries, up from 109 eligible titles a year ago. Across best film, director, the two screenplay races and the nine crafts, 213 features are in play. Count the titles entered only in specialty races such as Documentary, Animated Film or Outstanding Debut by a British Writer, Director or Producer and the list climbs to 235. Related Stories Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Billy Evans Writes Her an Emotional Thanksgiving Love Letter: ‘Our Most Beautiful Days Are Still Ahead of Us’ Chiwetel Ejiofor Was Afraid to Make ‘Backrooms’ Because of Director Kane Parsons’ Age: ‘He Was So Young!’

The list isn’t final. Distributors and producers have until noon GMT on Monday, Nov. 30, to request amendments and the official Entered Films List arrives Friday, Dec. 4, the same day Round One voting opens. Expect a few small corrections.

Among the list of films submitting in every category are Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three,” Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Emerald Fennell’s “Wuthering Heights,” Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” Robert Eggers’ “Werwulf,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple” and “Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man.”

Also swinging in all 12 categories are the Tom Cruise-vehicle “Digger,” “Verity,” “Send Help,” “Crime 101,” “The Death of Robin Hood,” “Heart of the Beast,” “Pressure,” “Ink,” “Tenzing,” “Wicker,” “The Sheep Detectives” and “Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.”
Then there’s “You Can See Everything.”

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary is entered in best film, director, documentary and seven of the nine craft races, including costume design and makeup and hair. What it doesn’t have is a single performance entry, and that’s because BAFTA rules deem it ineligible.

Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy playing Holmes in Hulu’s “The Dropout,” returns to the role in the A24 film’s dramatized reenactments, a performance Variety currently projects to win the Oscar for supporting actress. BAFTA joins the Golden Globes and Actor Awards (formerly the SAG Awards) among awards bodies where Seyfried is ineligible for recognition. Critics Choice stands alone in deeming her eligible for supporting actress, making it the only televised stop on the precursor circuit where she can be nominated. Critics Choice Awards nomination voting is underway.

articles.title: Oscar-Nominated Director Rachid Bouchareb on the Challenges of Shooting ‘Reggane’: ‘We’re Making a Period Film in the Depths of the Sahara’
paragraphs: Samir Guesmi joins cast as film gears up for April 2027 shoot

Among the challenges facing Franco-Algerian filmmaker Rachid Bouchareb as he prepares to shoot his next feature, “Reggane,” are rebuilding a French military base in the Algerian Sahara, sourcing military vehicles dating back to the final years of French colonial rule and dressing some 2,000 extras.

The three-time Oscar-nominated director, whose companion documentary short “Boomerang Atomic” is screening in the Ajyal Short Film Competition at the Doha Film Festival, tells Variety that the feature is now gearing up for an April 2027 shoot. “Each time, I discover that the scale of the production means preparation takes a little longer,” Bouchareb says. “We’re making a period film in the depths of the Sahara. There are surprises.” Related Stories Luca Guadagnino Wants Next Movie to Be a 'Love Story,' Confirms 'American Psycho’ and 'Separate Rooms’ Not Happening ‘Blade Runner 2099’ Boss Silka Luisa on What the Finale Means for Replicants and the Fate of Cora and Olwen

Set in 1960, two years before Algeria gained independence from France, the film follows an Algerian shepherd who dreams of becoming a fisherman but finds himself stuck on a French military base after the army requisitions him and his livestock.

Originally slated to begin shooting in September, the period drama is in preparation across a vast stretch of the Algerian Sahara, from south-central Timimoun, to Tamanrasset in the deep south and Djanet in the southeast. Some production locations are more than 1,200 miles from the coastal capital of Algiers, necessitating particularly complex logistical planning.
Algerian state-owned companies specializing in desert construction are working alongside the film’s art department to recreate the military base, while the Algerian army is supplying period vehicles.

Variety can exclusively reveal that French actor Samir Guesmi (“District B13”) is attached to the project. Further casting is underway to bring together professional Algerian and French actors alongside nonprofessional performers drawn from local communities.

Since Bouchareb unveiled the project to Variety last year, its financing structure has changed considerably. The feature is now financed entirely by Algerian partners, including the Ministry of Culture and Arts and the Algerian Center for Cinema Development (CADC), a public entity tasked with developing the country’s film industry. U.S.-based Cohen Media Group and Japan’s Kingyo Films are on board as co-production partners.

articles.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Soundtrack: The Best Music Moments From Haymitch Abernathy’s Prequel Movie
paragraphs: The “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” album is an absolute behemoth befitting the blockbuster movie.

With 29 entries ranging from in-movie needle drops and ditties written for the dystopian movie to existing songs remixed for the occasion, it’s longer than any previous “Hunger Games” soundtrack album. (“Mockingjay Part 2” leads with 19 tracks, “Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” clocks in at 17 songs, the original “Hunger Games” logs 16, and “Catching Fire” and “Mockingjay Part 1” both have 15.)

Noah Kahan joins Taylor Swift, Coldplay, Lorde and Olivia Rodrigo in a starry lineup of artists who have voiced the lead single for one of the franchise’s films. Kahan’s folk-Americana style blends into the rest of the soundtrack, which runs the gamut from country to indie. The soundtrack also includes songs from the movie’s stars, Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak and Katniss Everdeen herself, Jennifer Lawrence.

Writing lyrics for characters with lived experiences different from your own (i.e., fighting to the death in a televised cage match against other children) is no small task. Many of the “Sunrise on the Reaping” tracks capture the struggles of Haymitch Abernathy’s (Joseph Zada) games and the overarching resistance movement in Suzanne Collins’ franchise. Others are good, but could have been left on the cutting room floor (or saved for the artist’s own project).
If listening to nearly 30 songs seems daunting, Variety picked the 12 best moments that Hunger Games fans must dive into.

I imagine this is what most District 12 tributes think when their name is called on Reaping Day. Perhaps during the Quarter Quell Games that Haymitch enters, with twice as many tributes to face, the fight to the finish is even fiercer. And let’s not forget that classic Abernathy wisdom: “Nobody ever wins the Games, period. There are survivors … there’s no winners.” Stephen Wilson Jr.’s voice has a hint of twang and enough rasp to give this song the grittiness the situation demands; the bridge’s refrain of “I’ll keep running” builds into a final repetition with a desperate cry into an edgy final chorus that hammers that “last place” refrain until the end.

This song feels inspired by Haymitch’s (Zada) promise to Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak) that he will eventually see the sun rise on his birthday without a Reaping. It also rings of Wiress, whose mentorship centered around the idea that “all machines can be broken,” and the role the other rebellious Victors played in Katniss’ eventual success in ending the Hunger Games for good. And Lizzy McAlpine nails the right tone of rebellion here, which doesn’t hurt either. Her voice bends, rather than breaks, to steal some of this track’s lyrics, which deftly handles the shift between the angstier chorus and the arching vocals of the verses.

Sydney Rose clearly knows “Sunrise on the Reaping.” This is the song that perhaps most directly and accurately references the text: The mention of Lenore Dove’s geese with the birds chirping on the backing track, the boy “sent to slaughter,” the phone line the lovers speak through while Haymitch is in the Capitol, the liquor he finds respite in after the “biggest loss” that comes after thinking he had finally escaped the Arena. This song’s strength lies partly in its accuracy to the story and also in how gentle Rose’s vocals are over these lyrics, down to the devastating final line. It’s haunting, beautiful and it’s Haymitch mourning his lost love, sung with an angelic lilt to boot.

articles.title: Five-try Ireland beat Australia in autumn finale
paragraphs: Tries: Henshaw, Timoney, Baloucoune, McNabney 2 Cons: Prendergast 5 Pen: Prendergast
Ireland secured a fifth-place finish in the inaugural Nations Championship thanks to a 38-14 victory over Australia in London.
While last week's 20-17 win over South Africa was the undoubted highlight of their campaign, victory on Friday night ensured Ireland won all four games they played in November.
After Italy narrowly beat Fiji in the first game of the day, Ireland started slowly in a sparsely populated Allianz Stadium with the Wallabies taking a deserved lead through Jeremy Williams' try.

Andy Farrell's side took control of the contest through 24 unanswered points either side of half-time with Robbie Henshaw, Nick Timoney and Robert Baloucoune crossing for scores, while Sam Prendergast converted all three and added a penalty.

Kalani Thomas briefly stalled Ireland's momentum, but replacement back row James McNabney marked his second cap with a pair of tries in the final seven minutes to give the number two side in the world a comfortable, if not always convincing, victory.
After what was their final Test match of 2026, Ireland finish the year with a record of 10 wins and two losses from 12 internationals.
Nations Championship: Ireland ease past Australia at Allianz Stadium - reaction

articles.title: Decline of deities - the long game the All Blacks cannot afford to lose
paragraphs: Codie Taylor led the New Zealand haka against England before the 37-12 defeat last Saturday
Despite a population, player pool and bank balance smaller than most of their rivals, New Zealand's rugby team have become sporting shorthand for success.
England beat the All Blacks this year and last. They play them again on Saturday aiming for a hat-trick.
But, England would need that winning streak to continue until around 2050 just to level up a lop-sided historical head-to-head.
New Zealand have won 36 times to England's 10 in their 121-year rivalry.
For every other nation in Test rugby, the story is the same. New Zealand have the superior record against them all.
A section on the All Blacks' website, titled Rivalries,, external opens by listing South Africa's 40% winning record in their meetings. And the numbers only drop from there.
But New Zealand's grip on the global game appears looser now than ever.

articles.title: Gibbs-White stars, Fofana struggles - player ratings for Forest v Chelsea
paragraphs: Premier League highlights: Nottingham Forest 3-2 Chelsea
Morgan Gibbs-White scored twice as Nottingham Forest beat Chelsea at the City Ground for the first time since 1997.
Igor Jesus' brilliant volley opened the scoring after just five minutes, before Gibbs-White struck twice in the second half as Chelsea were consigned to a fourth defeat in five matches.
Forest ran out 3-2 winners despite Emmanuel Emegha twice pulling goals back.
Here's how I rated the players and how you rated the players.
Matz Sels: The Belgian goalkeeper could do little about Emegha's goals but did not need to make many saves. 6
Jair Cunha: Cunha made one brilliant last-ditch tackle in the second half as Chelsea pushed for an equaliser. 7
Nikola Milenkovic: The Serbian was solid in the middle of the back three but otherwise unremarkable. 7

articles.title: Mercedes set pace in eventful Qatar second practice
paragraphs: World champion Kimi Antonelli set the pace ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell in a disrupted second practice at the Qatar Grand Prix.
Italian Antonelli was 0.127 seconds quicker than Russell on the medium tyre, as neither driver set a time on the soft compound because of two red flags that punctuated the session.
Lewis Hamilton also came to halt after his Ferrari lost power, with a virtual safety car deployed so the marshals could come to the seven-time world champion's aid.

The McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri plus Red Bull's Max Verstappen completed the top five at the Lusail International Circuit, with the trio setting soft-tyre times that were more than four tenths adrift of the two Mercedes.
The first red flag was to clear gravel off the track after an incident for Ferrari's Charles Leclerc early on, while the other was to recover the Alpine of Pierre Gasly following a high-speed spin.
Frenchman Gasly hit a marker board before beaching himself after taking too much kerb at Turn 14 in the middle of the qualifying simulation runs.
The interruptions led to the second hour being extended by 13 minutes to allow drivers more time on track in the representative conditions.
"It was a productive day," said Antonelli. "We tried a lot of things on the car between FP1 and FP2, but in FP2, it seemed like we did a step back with the car.

articles.title: Cricket Australia may not like sandpaper forum findings - Vaughan
paragraphs: Cameron Bancroft (left) was caught using sandpaper on the ball during Australia's third Test in South Africa in 2018
Cricket Australia (CA) will not like what it finds from a forum into the sandpaper scandal, according to former England captain Michael Vaughan.
CA has invited evidence into the ball-tampering controversy of Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018 following weeks of speculation over which players and coaches were involved.
"It's very clear to me that Cricket Australia are going to find some things out that they're probably not going to want to find out," Vaughan told the Test Match Special podcast.
"If they don't release the truth of what they find in this forum out to the public, we're going to get back to square one."
The row over the ball-tampering scandal was reignited by claims published in the autobiography of former Australia batter Usman Khawaja.
At the time of the controversy, only batter Cameron Bancroft, then captain Steve Smith and his deputy David Warner were punished for the cheating plot.
Khawaja alleged all players and coaches knew of the tampering and should have taken responsibility, a testimony supported by Bancroft, Warner and squad players Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland.

articles.title: Wilshere v Ramsey - Arsenal legends treading similar managerial paths
paragraphs: Jack Wilshere and Aaron Ramsey are the third and fourth youngest managers across the 92 Premier League and EFL clubs
Both were midfield prodigies. Both won the FA Cup playing for Arsenal under Arsene Wenger. Both represented their countries.

The image of the pair celebrating Ramsey's extra-time winner together in the 2014 FA Cup final against Hull City to end Arsenal's nine-year trophy drought at the time will forever be ingrained in the north London club's history.
They were teenagers when they made their Premier League debuts for the Gunners on the same day just two minutes apart as substitutes in a 4-0 win at Blackburn in September 2008.
Aged just 16 and 17, each were considered hot prospects who would go on to have excellent careers - and so it proved in many ways, even if both were restricted by injuries along the way.
Now 34 and 35, their paths cross again under different circumstances but many similarities very much still remain.
They are both in League One in their first permanent managerial jobs. And, guess what? Both their sides are in fine form and vying for promotion to the Championship.
It will be the first time they have met as permanent managers when Wilshere's Luton Town host Ramsey's Oxford United at Kenilworth Road on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

articles.title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
paragraphs: There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.
Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.
"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.
Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

articles.title: From £250 job to £9,000 bill: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
paragraphs: Nessar Khawaja told almost 70,000 social media followers his network makes money from "desperate" customers
Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found.

Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers, and recruiting online to expand his network.
"Me and my team, we're top of the food chain," he said in one video.
The investigation found the 23-year-old is a key figure within an organised group that is systematically ripping off customers and teaching others to do the same.
The BBC put these allegations to Khawaja in writing. He denied any wrongdoing and said his social media posts were intended as light-hearted comedy that did not reflect how he operated in practice.
In a recorded phone call, Khawaja insisted he was an entertainer, was joking and that the BBC had "taken things out of context".
In another video, Khawaja made claims he had electricians working for him who made more than £40,000 a month.

articles.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
paragraphs: The UK has agreed the deals in a bid to cut red tape for British companies
The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.
The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.
It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.
Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

articles.title: Asia made a big AI bet on Nvidia. What happens now?
paragraphs: Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?
Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.
Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.

Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.

The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.
From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.
In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.
That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.

articles.title: My self-care ritual is a meal at a fancy restaurant - on my own
paragraphs: Self-confessed foodie Catherine has booked tables for one in the UK and abroad

Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat opposite - bliss.
"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.
The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.
As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."
We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.
Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.
She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.

articles.title: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
paragraphs: Jim Lembesis has been working on elevators in Chicago for 47 years
Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here.

When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again.
"They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?"

The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started."
Lift and escalator technicians "amaze" with their ability to fix things
Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped, external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.

articles.title: Inflation has shoppers hunting for value. That bodes well for Black Friday
paragraphs: Economic headwinds have made consumers more cautious — but new data and reports from retailers are painting a picture of robust holiday spending through Black Friday and beyond.

The macroeconomic environment has squeezed wallets. High inflation, fluctuating gas prices and labor uncertainty have dampened consumer sentiment and contributed to a pullback in spending. October's consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, coming in higher than expected, while the personal consumption expenditures price index accelerated to a seasonally adjusted 3.8% in October compared with last year. Meanwhile, October retail sales grew at their slowest pace in nearly a year, according to the CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor.

The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index slid to its lowest since 2014 in September, with respondents citing concerns about inflation and the job market. It's translated into caution from some retailers like Walmart and Lowe's, which have reported slower sales, smaller baskets and drops in big-ticket and discretionary purchases.
Despite that pullback, recent earnings reports and end-of-year forecasts suggest consumers are still willing to shell out for the holidays.

Planned spending on gifts and nongifts is estimated to be $1,049 on average this year, up 5.9% from $990 last year, according to The Conference Board. Adjusting for inflation, that figure is still up 3.2% year over year.

Holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion this year, but that growth is boosted by inflation. Though consumers have said they're willing to spend, experts have noted that shoppers are still emphasizing value and looking for deals where they can. Adobe data found that in the first 22 days of November — what it considers the beginning of the holiday season — consumers spent $82.5 billion online, marking a 9.1% year-over-year increase.

That's translating to the Black Friday and Cyber Monday week, too, as consumers take advantage of deals that started days before the traditional Friday blitz. Salesforce is predicting a record-breaking holiday week between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, as it expects online sales to reach $357 billion globally and $84 billion in the U.S., both marking 6% year-over-year increases.
The report also found that retailers are offering bigger markdowns than last year, with discount rates up 8% in the U.S. in November.

articles.title: Trump demands probe into 'record setting error' after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher
paragraphs: President Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."

Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate. That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.

That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post, suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and multiple governorships.

"I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.

However, the difference between the advance estimate and the figure in the second release is far from being an all-time record. It was the largest revision since the 1.2 percentage point revision seen in the second quarter of 2020.

On an absolute basis, the latest revision was tied for 16th among all revisions from the advance estimate to the second release since 1990. It also tied four other quarters with a similar 0.9 percentage point difference — and was approximately double the average revision of 0.43 percentage points for all 147 quarters.
The upward revision shows Trump's policies are "delivering results" that defy expectations, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC.

Revisions to U.S. economic numbers are not out of the ordinary. Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. That data is later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.

articles.title: The S&P 500 is in a correction. Bear markets and recessions don't always follow
paragraphs: The S&P 500 fell into a correction on Nov. 20 for the first time since April 2025 as stocks pulled back sharply from October's record highs.

The market correction, defined as a 10% decline from a recent high, came as investor concern mounted over a potential slowdown in AI spending, mega-cap tech valuations and the path of Federal Reserve interest rate policy. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Nov. 20 alone, closing at 6,910.39, its seventh consecutive daily decline. That left the index 11.6% below the Oct. 6 closing high of 7,818.93.

A correction can deepen into a bear market, defined as a drop of 20% or more from the most recent top. But history shows that even a bear market, let alone a correction, doesn't automatically mean the economy is destined for a recession.

In a CNBC analysis, eight of the 13 S&P 500 bear markets overlapped with recessions, as defined by the National Bureau of Economic Research, and five did not. The NBER says a recession is "a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months."

The 1973-74 oil shock, the dot-com bust in 2000, the 2007-09 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic downturn all overlapped with recessions. But some major bear markets also occurred without one, including in 1987 and 2022.

Deutsche Bank macro strategist Henry Allen said that every S&P 500 bear market since the 1962 "Kennedy Slide" has coincided with at least one of three factors: a recession, worsening economic data raising recession fears, or a cycle of Federal Reserve rate hikes. None of those are present today, at least so far.

"Much as last week's selloff was severe, it's worth remembering that it has several differences with many of the other big risk-off moves in recent times," the London-based strategist wrote on Tuesday.

Allen said there hasn't been any sudden reassessment of the growth outlook recently, which happened during the Covid-19 shock, when the pandemic pushed the global economy into recession and the S&P 500 plunged 33.9% in just 33 days. Nor is the current situation similar to the 2025 "Liberation Day" tariff period either, which also prompted a reassessment of the growth outlook.

articles.title: Budget airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy in Europe after failing to secure funding
paragraphs: Budget carrier Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy Friday, saying it failed to secure funding after soaring fuel costs strained the company's operations throughout the year.
Its parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, concluded that the Norwegian carrier no longer has a basis to continue operations.
"Despite extensive efforts, the Company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs," the firm said in a statement Friday.

It comes days after Norse said it's facing a "critical financial situation" and was considering its options from a strategic takeover to ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. The company's shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.
The board has now filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court, where a trustee will be appointed to manage the process further.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the Company and the Group to find a solution," Norse Atlantic CEO Eivind Roald said.

"We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners. The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald added.
The company has canceled all flights, and ticket sales have been discontinued.

articles.title: Chinese chip stocks notch biggest ever one-day gains as Beijing signals broader market support
paragraphs: Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.

The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT, Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.

The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.

articles.title: Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers
paragraphs: Ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies. Beyond its natural presence in sunlight, it is used to disinfect surfaces, make biological materials fluoresce, and manufacture computer chips through a process called photolithography. In the future, microscopic sources of UV light built directly into photonic chips could enable smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and other advanced technologies.

However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge. Ultraviolet light rapidly loses power as it travels through optical waveguides, the tiny channels that carry light across a chip. This limitation has made it extremely difficult to develop compact UV sources with enough power for practical applications.

Now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices. The researchers, working in the laboratory of Marko Lončar, the Tiantsai Lin Professor of Electrical Engineering, achieved the breakthrough using a widely studied material called thin-film lithium niobate.
Published in Nature Communications, the findings establish lithium niobate as a promising platform for generating powerful ultraviolet light in compact devices while minimizing optical losses.
Rather than trying to deliver ultraviolet light directly through microscopic channels, the researchers designed a device that generates UV light from red light within the chip itself.

The approach relies on a process known as frequency upconversion. Inside the lithium niobate crystal, two photons of red light combine to produce a single ultraviolet photon with higher energy. Lithium niobate is particularly well suited to this process because of its exceptional ability to convert light from one frequency to another.
"Our group is perhaps best known for utilizing lithium niobate for photonic devices that operate at longer, infrared wavelengths -- closer to the realm of telecommunications signals," Lončar said.
