However, the team found that this transparent crystalline material, which has become increasingly important in integrated photonics, can also support light sources and guide light at much shorter wavelengths, including those in the ultraviolet range.

articles.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
paragraphs: In the 17th century, Danish King Frederik III already knew that the legendary unicorn horn came from a real animal. However, this creature had fins instead of hooves and inhabited the icy waters of the Arctic. The king dispatched an expedition to Greenland to investigate the source of these highly prized objects. The successful mission earned him a throne fashioned entirely from "unicorn horns," enhancing his power and prestige across Europe. Yet the treasured horn was not actually a horn, but "merely" a tooth.

The narwhal's tusk is unlike almost any other tooth in nature. Whereas elongated teeth, including elephant and walrus tusks and beaver incisors, grow in curved shapes, the male narwhal develops a remarkable corkscrew-shaped tooth. Typically, the upper left canine grows forward through the upper lip, twisting counterclockwise as it extends. It can reach two meters (6.6 feet) in length, equivalent to as much as half the animal's body length.

This unusual biological structure caught the attention of an international team of researchers from several scientific disciplines. Using advanced X-ray imaging techniques, they set out to determine whether the arrangement of the tusk's microscopic building blocks could explain the direction of its visible spiral.

What they discovered was even more remarkable than expected. Rather than forming a single spiral, the tusk's tiny structural components create two intertwined helices that twist in opposite directions. Together, they produce an exceptionally stable structure.

The research was conducted at three major European synchrotron facilities: the Swiss Light Source SLS at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen, the MAX IV Laboratory in Lund (Sweden), and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility ESRF in Grenoble (France). The findings were published in Nature Communications.

Narwhal tusks continue growing throughout the animals' lives and can easily reach 70 years of age. Despite their striking appearance, the precise purpose of these enormous teeth remains uncertain. Evidence suggests they are primarily involved in mate selection. Narwhals have also been observed crossing their tusks in playful "duels," supporting the idea that the structures are important for reproduction and social interactions.
Although questions remain about how narwhals use their tusks, scientists now have a much clearer picture of how they are constructed.

"Like bones or other teeth in the animal kingdom, the narwhal tusk is a complex composite material whose structure extends from tiny nanoscale building blocks to the visible form of the entire tooth," says Marianne Liebi, a PSI researcher and co-author of the study.

articles.title: A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles
paragraphs: Researchers have identified a naturally occurring molecule that plays a crucial role in building muscle strength and improving physical performance. Released during exercise, the molecule could also provide the basis for future treatments to protect against muscle damage associated with type 2 diabetes.

The molecule, known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), is essential for muscles to adapt to physical activity. It helps muscles become stronger, improves their resistance to fatigue, and protects against damage and weakness.

The study, published in Nature Communications and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), reveals that L-BAIBA is a central regulator of the biological changes that allow muscles to improve their strength, structure, and endurance in response to exercise training.

Although the health benefits of exercise are well established, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that allow the body to adapt to physical demands. A research team led by Professor Lee Roberts at the University of Leeds investigated whether these processes could reveal new ways to treat chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes.

L-BAIBA has attracted scientific interest for more than a decade. In research published in 2014, Roberts demonstrated that the molecule has beneficial effects on metabolism, helping to enhance the body's ability to burn fat in response to exercise. L-BAIBA is now commercially available as a dietary supplement.

The latest findings reveal another important function of the molecule. L-BAIBA acts as a chemical messenger that connects physical activity with beneficial changes in muscle structure and metabolism, helping muscles adapt to the demands placed on them.

Lee Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said: "Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance.

"This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes."

articles.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
paragraphs: Old plumbing pipes, discarded window frames, and expired credit cards could one day become valuable ingredients in engine oil. Researchers at Virginia Tech have developed a new chemical process that transforms one of the world's most difficult plastics to recycle into a high-performance lubricant material.

Led by chemist and chemical engineer Guoliang "Greg" Liu, the research team discovered how to convert polyvinyl chloride (PVC) into polyalphaolefin, a key ingredient in synthetic lubricants such as engine oil.

Published in the journal Nature, the research offers a potential solution to two environmental challenges: reducing the accumulation of stubborn plastic waste and finding more sustainable ways to manufacture valuable industrial lubricants.

PVC is particularly difficult to recycle because of its chlorine content and the wide range of chemical additives manufacturers incorporate into their products. These additives can give PVC different properties, such as flexibility, rigidity, and resistance to heat. However, they also complicate conventional recycling methods. Consequently, much of the world's discarded PVC ends up in landfills.

Meanwhile, global demand for lubricants continues to grow, and producing these materials can come with significant environmental costs. Transforming discarded PVC into a valuable lubricant ingredient could help address both problems.

Although lubricants rarely attract much attention, they are essential to modern machinery. They reduce friction and wear between moving components, helping engines operate efficiently and extending the lifespan of mechanical equipment. Everything from lawn mowers and passenger vehicles to jet engines depends on reliable lubricants.
The Virginia Tech team's process could provide an alternative source of these important materials while helping address the growing problem of plastic pollution.

To make the lubricant, researchers place PVC of the kind commonly used in household plumbing, window frames, and credit cards into a solvent. They then introduce aluminum trichloride and alpha-olefins, a class of hydrocarbons used in the manufacture of synthetic lubricants. The mixture is heated to 158 degrees Fahrenheit for three hours, after which the researchers extract a relatively thick lubricating oil.

articles.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
paragraphs: Screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized. A new study tracking children from age 1 to 8 found that those who spent more time watching screens during infancy and around the start of elementary school tended to perform worse academically at age 9 and have weaker working memory at age 10.5.

The findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as important as how much time they spend in front of them. Two ages in particular, 1 and 6, emerged as potentially sensitive periods in childhood development.

As digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority. Recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the American Academy of Pediatrics generally emphasize avoiding screen exposure during the first 18 to 24 months of life and limiting it to less than one hour a day for children ages 2 to 5. However, many young children spend considerably more time using screens.

Despite growing concerns about children's digital habits, previous research has produced mixed findings about the relationship between screen time and cognitive development. Many earlier studies examined children at a single point in time, concentrated on children already attending school, or did not regularly track screen habits throughout early childhood.

Following the same children over several years allows researchers to investigate whether screen exposure at particular ages is more strongly associated with later outcomes. This approach can also help researchers better account for the influence of family circumstances and environmental factors.

Scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore addressed these gaps in a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics. The researchers examined data from 502 children participating in the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) birth cohort.

Parents reported their children's screen viewing habits at six different points between infancy and middle childhood. The researchers then evaluated the children's academic achievement and working memory several years later.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and manipulate information. It plays an essential role in everyday learning, allowing children to follow instructions, solve math problems, understand sentences, and keep track of information while completing tasks.

articles.title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease
paragraphs: A familiar dietary supplement combined with low-dose aspirin may offer an unexpected alternative to antibiotics for people with severe gum disease. In a year-long clinical trial, patients who received omega-3 and aspirin alongside conventional periodontal treatment experienced nearly identical clinical benefits to those who received antibiotics. Perhaps even more surprisingly, the improvements were still evident six months after supplementation ended.

The findings, published in the Journal of Periodontology, come from researchers affiliated with Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital, Guarulhos University (UNG), the University of Taubaté (UNITAU), and the Ribeirão Preto School of Dentistry at USP (FORP-USP) in Brazil, as well as Harvard University in the United States.

The study suggests that combining omega-3 with low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), better known as aspirin, could reduce the need for antibiotics in certain patients. The discovery is particularly timely given growing worldwide concerns about antibiotic resistance, which occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive exposure to drugs designed to kill them.

Researchers monitored 109 patients with advanced periodontitis over 12 months. Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease that develops when bacteria accumulate below the gumline, triggering an immune response that can gradually damage the tissues and bone that hold teeth in place. Without proper treatment, the disease can cause teeth to loosen and eventually fall out.

As periodontitis progresses, spaces known as periodontal pockets form between the teeth and gums. These pockets can become increasingly deep, making it difficult to remove harmful bacteria through ordinary brushing and flossing.

"Patients with severe disease have very deep pockets, which act as reservoirs for bacteria associated with the disease. It's a very challenging condition to treat," says dental surgeon Nídia Cristina Castro dos Santos, the first author of the study and a professor and researcher at Einstein.

The researchers randomly divided the participants into four treatment groups. Every patient received subgingival instrumentation, commonly referred to as scaling. This standard periodontal treatment involves removing bacterial deposits and hardened plaque from tooth surfaces beneath the gums. Each group also received a different complementary treatment.
Patients in the control group received inactive substitutes for the antibiotics, omega-3, and aspirin, supplied in capsules that looked identical to those containing the active treatments.

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power a day after US slammed with Thanksgiving storms
paragraphs: Watch: Severe Thanksgiving storms leave roads flooded and trees fallen
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.

Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.
Conditions are now improving, though forecasters caution that it will take some time. The West Coast also was affected by its own storms.
Flight disruption persisted, too, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - another busy travel day.
More than 2,700 flights within, into, or out of the US were delayed and nearly 150 cancelled on Friday.

On Thanksgiving, more than 2,500 US flights were delayed and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com. One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

articles.title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
paragraphs: An official inspects the partially submerged tanker - the rescue operation is expected to be challenging
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.
All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.
There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.
The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".
"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.

articles.title: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinking
paragraphs: Four million people in Lagos, Nigeria may be exposed to extreme sea levels by the end of the century, a new study says
Some of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.
Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.

The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.
Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".
This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change.
Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.

articles.title: Severe Thanksgiving storms leave roads flooded and trees fallen
paragraphs: Both US coasts have been battered by severe Thanksgiving storms, leaving behind flooded roads, fallen trees, and widespread power outages for hundreds of thousands of people.
Although the weather is expected to improve, hundreds of flights remain delayed or cancelled on Friday.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the east Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

articles.title: 'Can't control the weather': Sadness as Macy's Thanksgiving parade postponed
paragraphs: Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York because of severe weather. It is the first time the parade has been postponed due to weather.
Fans and volunteers voiced their disappointment over the postponement, with one remarking: 'We can't control the weather!'

Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.
It is hoped the parade will take place on Saturday instead.

articles.title: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
paragraphs: An official holds one of the seized Vallarta mud turtles - they are now receiving care at a specialised sanctuary
Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.
The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.
It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.
The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.
Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.

articles.title: Artemis III Astronaut Andre Douglas Visits VAB
paragraphs: NASA astronaut Andre Douglas, Artemis III mission specialist, stands inside an RS-25 engine test article during a visit to the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026.

During Artemis III, four RS-25 engines will power the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket core stage to send the Orion spacecraft to conduct critical rendezvous and docking tests with lunar lander systems in low Earth orbit, advancing the capabilities needed before astronauts return to the lunar surface on Artemis IV.

articles.title: NASA’s NG-25 Mission to Launch Pioneering Space Crops Research
paragraphs: NASA experiments, including a first-of-its-kind space crop production system, will travel to the International Space Station aboard Northrop Grumman’s 25th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency.
Investigations from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division will advance research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration, expanding knowledge of space crops and human health.

Astronauts will need sustainable sources of food to travel farther and stay longer in space. To help understand how crop production works in microgravity, NASA is launching a novel space crops experiment.

The new prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing safe, nutritious, and reliable crop production systems for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions. Knowledge gained from the space crop production system also could help inform agricultural practices such as vertical farming and indoor growing systems.
Researchers will use this investigation to validate the system’s water delivery and volume optimization technology aboard the space station.
A precision health investigation is the next step toward enabling long-duration studies of human brain tissues in space.

The research builds on a previous investigation that sent small, lab-grown models of the human brain, called miBrains, to the space station. This experiment will validate a miniature fluid-handling system designed to mix, deliver, and maintain the nutrient-rich liquid needed to keep the tissues alive.

Researchers could use the findings to help identify potential neurological risks associated with spaceflight and develop strategies to protect astronaut health. It also may advance human tissue research and neurological disease modeling on Earth.

articles.title: APOD: 2026 November 27 – The Moon Watchers
paragraphs: Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Explanation: On November 24, all denizens of our fair planet could watch the Moon rise opposite the setting Sun. Easy to spot in twilight skies above fields, fences, backyards, and even stone walls, the Moon was big and bright, and at its full phase. Known to some as a Beaver Moon, November's Full Moon was also near perigee, the closest point in its elliptical orbit around planet Earth. That made it one of the biggest and brightest Full Moons, also known as a supermoon. In fact, November's Full Moon was the first in a series of four consecutive Full Moons near perigee. So your next chance to watch a supermoon rise will be when the Cold Moon rises on December 23.Tomorrow's picture: remember where you parked

articles.title: Shivelyuch Socked In
paragraphs: A cloud layer encircled the flanks of the volcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula but left its restless summit caldera in view.

In the same way that Shivelyuch (also called Shiveluch) frequently displays volcanic activity, it is also chronically obscured by clouds. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes.

The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome, formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows.

In November 2026, effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity at Shivelyuch had been ongoing for months, according to reports from the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT). And despite frequent cloudiness, satellites regularly detect thermal anomalies from the volcano.

On the day of this image, KVERT reported that a plume of resuspended ash drifted 120 kilometers (75 miles) to the east. That kind of activity is relatively tame for the mountain. Explosions from Shivelyuch periodically send ash several kilometers up into the atmosphere, where it can travel great distances and pose risks to aircraft. In July 2026, an ash plume rode the jet stream over the Bering Sea into Alaskan airspace, according to news reports, prompting the cancellation of multiple flights.
NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Lindsey Doermann.
Stay up-to-date with the latest content from NASA as we explore the universe and discover more about our home planet.
A powerful eruption from the Indonesian volcano lofted ash into the atmosphere, disrupting thousands of flights and degrading air quality.

paragraphs: Skip the cheap junk. We found Black Friday deals on investment-grade products that will still be ticking for many Thanksgivings to come
Our favorite bath towel is already on sale for Black Friday

paragraphs: It is already cold – but if you put off winter shopping as I did, these Black Friday deals may help

Lately, it feels as if I blinked and that late autumn weather reared its ugly (cold, damp) head. If you, like me, repeatedly procrastinate auditing your winter gear only to realize belatedly that your boots have holes in them and much of your outerwear can best be described as a light statement layer (the jacket is the outfit, after all), you have come to the right place.

We should be screwed. It’s getting cold and winter gear is in demand. Brands have little business incentive to slash prices right now except that, well, it’s Black Friday! The deals below are all backed up by our own testing.

You may want to size up, as well. Amazon reports some returns due to it feeling too snug.

This warm yet breathable merino wool top is a favorite of our outdoor reviewer Paige Triola, who put it to the test with a day on the slopes in Breckenridge, Colorado. “These base layers provided just the right amount of warmth and didn’t get stinky after a full day of playing in the snow,” she said when they went on sale in May.

I am not being hyperbolic when I say three out of four people in my tundra-like neighborhood resort to a Super Puff coat to survive Canadian winters. Filter editorial coordinator Lauren Gould loves hers too: “For the past few winters, I’ve relied on my Aritzia Super Puff to keep me warm and toasty while commuting on foot to the office and running errands,” she said in our guide to the best Black Friday fashion deals. At $220, it’s cheaper than it has been all year.

These Vuori joggers are my catch-all pants of choice come winter: they’re cozy enough to curl up in, yet performance-driven enough to absorb moisture and let my skin breathe when I decide to bang out a couple reps. Some of the sizes and colors are already picked over, so check both retailers if you can’t find the combo you want.

articles.title: We found 17 Black Friday deals on plastic-free products we’ve tried and loved
paragraphs: Reduce your exposure to microplastics and Pfas with these Filter-tested picks that are on sale now for Black Friday
Reducing your exposure to plastic is a good idea. We don’t yet know all the ways plastics can harm us or the environment, but we are discovering alarming things all the time.

If you can swing a plastic-free life, or reduce your plastic use in strategic ways, you will limit your exposure to potentially harmful chemicals (including forever chemicals, which are known to potentially disrupt the endocrine system). As an added benefit, you will also probably help conserve our planet’s natural resources, reduce fossil fuel emissions and protect marine life, among other things.
While going plastic-free often comes at a premium, we have rounded up a bunch of plastic-free products we’ve tested that are on sale during Black Friday and Cyber Monday this year.

We test products here at the Filter US and handpicked these deals. You can learn more about us at the bottom of the list. Products marked (sold out) are out of stock or no longer discounted. We’ll update our guides throughout Black Friday.

Out of all 15 blenders kitchen expert Marian Bull tested, this decidedly nostalgic one from Oster earned top marks for its “most plastic-free” construction. “If you’re looking for a blender that will minimize potential exposure to microplastics, this is a great option, thanks to its glass jug,” she said. “The lid is still plastic, but has less contact with your food.”

Quit throwing away plastic bags with this pack of six Stasher silicone food storage bags, now a couple bucks shy of their lowest price this year. “An investment in a Stasher bag is one that will more than pay for itself,” wrote our kitchen expert Megan Wahn when a smaller set went on sale last year.

If your crunchy plastic shower curtain is starting to mildew, consider this breathable Brooklinen linen shower curtain, which reviewer Stephen Treffinger praised for its casual vibe when he tested the best shower curtains. Just be prepared to iron it, if you don’t like the shabby chic look.

articles.title: We found 21 Black Friday deals on the day-to-day essentials everyone uses
paragraphs: Stock up on boring basics this Black Friday – you’ll thank yourself later

When you think about all the items on your Black Friday wishlist, toilet paper and dish soap probably won’t crack the top 10. From a pair of reliable scissors to stash in that junk drawer that will last decades to an odor eliminator that can make even that nastiest of litter boxes smell fresh, here are some household staples to save a few bucks on.

For the last two years, I’ve felt better washing my kids’ dishware with these pods, which contain no dyes, sulfates, or phosphates. They also leave glass and china so sparkling clean it’s as if a busboy at a bougie restaurant manually dried them with a cloth.

Unsure of how to treat a stubborn stain? Take cues from stylist Liz Teich, who told us this non-toxic stain remover is her “holy grail” for all kinds of mysterious stains. The kit comes with a brush to dig deeper into fibers. You’ll see the 25% discount when you add it to your cart.

They even made the UK Filter’s guide to thoughtful gifts that won’t end up in a landfill. “Barely a day goes by when I’m not opening the kitchen drawer to pull one or the other out,” said one giftee of these hardworking, orange-handled scissors she received as a gift in the 1980s.

articles.title: Too old for soft toys? Tell that to kidults booking up the Harrods Jellycat cafe
paragraphs: Department stores are hosting in-person events for those who find comfort in collecting the British soft toy brand
They’re cute, cuddly and taking over the homes of young adults.

Jellycat, a British soft toy brand founded in 1999, is experiencing a rise in interest from adult buyers as they snap up signature smiley designs in the shape of everything from croissants and disco balls to turtles and teabags.

The trend is part of a wider “kidult” movement, with grownups buying items traditionally geared towards children, for example, Lego sets and Pokémon cards. On social media, videos of users talking through their collections of soft toys known as plushies can rack up millions of views.

On Monday, Harrods in London is opening “a first-of-its-kind dining destination” – a Jellycat cafe serving brunch in edible and soft toy form. Diners will be able to buy a peach granola bowl-shaped plushie, and eat the dish too.

According to research by Circana, “kidult” toy sales in the UK grew 22% in the first half of 2026. One in five toys and games are now bought by over-18s for themselves. At the US department chain Nordstrom, the average age of a Jellycat buyer is 27. Everything from nostalgia to a rise in anxiety disorders is being credited as a contributing factor to the trend.

Audrey Tang, a chartered member of the British Psychological Society, describes Jellycats as “tactile, comforting, calming and very cutesy”. She isn’t surprised to see increased demand from adults for plushies. “This year has been tough on a lot of people so if there is anything that makes us smile or makes us feel nice, we’re probably going to choose that,” she says.

Tang dismisses age-regression concerns, saying it is a type of judgment. “Try thinking about where that voice about rules is coming from,” she says. “Often those types of judgments come from parents or caregivers who have previously told us: ‘You’re too old for this or you should grow out of that.’”

articles.title: NHS boss warns of 'horrible spike' in flu as hospital admissions surge
paragraphs: A surge in severe cases of flu has prompted health officials in England to urge those most at risk to get vaccinated as soon as possible.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said hospital admission rates had soared by almost 80% over the last week to the highest at this time of year since before the Covid pandemic.

Flu vaccine uptake so far among those aged 65 and over was just under 68% - lower than where it usually was at this time of year, the agency said. The flu can be very serious for those living with some long-term health conditions.
Outgoing chief executive for NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, talked of how some hospitals had introduced mask-wearing to stem the spread of respiratory illnesses.
Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".
"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.
However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.

articles.title: Reform UK pledges to scrap hospital parking fees in England
paragraphs: Reform UK is promising to scrap parking fees at NHS hospitals in England for all patients, visitors, and staff if it wins power at the next election.
The party said rising parking charges in recent years were unfair, with some hospitals charging up to £20 a day for parking spots.
It says it would compensate hospital trusts for the £300m they currently get from fees each year by raising more from foreign visitors using the NHS.
The health department said it expected charges to be reasonable, with fees used to maintain facilities or put towards funding health services.

Reform's announcement is part of a broader effort by the party to win credibility on the NHS, as it prepares to appoint someone who has worked in the NHS as its health spokesperson in the coming weeks.
Leader Nigel Farage's previous support for an insurance-based healthcare model has harmed the party's standing on the health service, insiders admit.

The latest policy is also part of a series designed to improve the party's recent struggles in the polls by addressing what Reform see as their perceived weaknesses, on Russia, on defence and now the NHS.

Reform's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick told the BBC the party's spending plans would be set closer to an election, but the party would ensure there would always be "real-terms increases" in funding for the NHS.

articles.title: Private dentists too expensive for millions, watchdog warns
paragraphs: The Competition watchdog says wide-ranging reforms are needed in the UK's private dentistry market to ensure people get a fair deal.
It says patients can struggle with costs and find it difficult to shop around and compare prices.
Around four million people did not go to the dentist in the past two years because they found treatment expensive, the watchdog estimates.
The British Dental Association says it is essential that there is a thriving private market but it is also vital that the government fixes NHS dentistry.

The Competition and Markets Authority's (CMA) interim report on private dentist services says millions of people are struggling with the costs of private dental care, with some delaying or going without treatment.
Private dentist services are now used by about 60% of UK patients for some care
At large dental groups prices rose by around 7% a year on average between 2023 and 2025, ahead of inflation and wage increases
A composite white filling is equivalent to about 36% of average weekly disposable income in the North East of England and 35% in Wales

articles.title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
paragraphs: Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.

According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.

As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
paragraphs: It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.

GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).
The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.

Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”
Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.

“We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.
That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI.
“We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”

articles.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
paragraphs: A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.
Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.
Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

articles.title: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
paragraphs: The Med Emre vessel capsized near Ibiza and Spain's Clara Campoamor, a pollution control vessel, was sent to assess the environmental impact
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.

The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of Valencia, told news agency AFP that a small slick that had formed around the boat had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out on Friday morning.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
paragraphs: Gérard Depardieu has faced a series of allegations in recent years on film sets and elsewhere
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.

articles.title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel. And, FCC violated ABC's free speech, judge says
paragraphs: Your support helps make our show possible and unlocks access to our sponsor-free feed.

Severe storms sweeping across the nation threaten to cause widespread travel delays today, as millions of people gather with their loved ones. New York City officials announced that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled to Saturday due to the threat of powerful wind gusts that could reach up to 60 mph. This year marked the 100th procession, and the first time the iconic event is being postponed.

Workers inflate the Spider-Man balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 on November 25, 2026 in New York City. Macy's plans to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables, but forecasted high winds are threatening to ground the giant balloons. Adam Gray/Getty Images hide caption

The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs targeting goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. Administration officials argue the measures counter unfair foreign trade practices, though critics question their ultimate effectiveness. Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.

Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in Eastern Iowa for lead contamination after the U.S. Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown yesterday. Officials said the controlled explosion was the only safe way to dispose of the bomb-making compound.

A federal judge has blocked Trump from challenging the ABC television network's broadcast licenses. U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan ruled that the president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional. AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction yesterday and dismissed the administration's request to throw out ABC and Disney's lawsuit challenging the review of the local license. Licenses typically last eight years and are rarely revoked. AliKhan's decision drew heavily on Trump's public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, as well as comments from Brendan Carr, the president's pick for chair of the Federal Communications Commission.
Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible. J Studios/Getty Images hide caption

Holiday shopping season is in full swing. Before you spend, consider if you actually need what's in your cart. Sales are exciting because our brains are wired to seek newness. Retailers capitalize on that urge. To escape the cycle of constantly wanting more, shop intentionally and appreciate what you already own, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New. He shares his insights on breaking this cycle and finding joy in your current possessions with Life Kit.

articles.title: How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
paragraphs: Yvonne Capehart Weah's family routinely gets together in the township where she grew up in Liberia. In early November every year, they gather to celebrate the Liberian version of Thanksgiving. Eddie Raynes hide caption
Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.
That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

articles.title: Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.
paragraphs: Your support helps make our show possible and unlocks access to our sponsor-free feed.

The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.
A sign hangs from a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, on Nov. 23, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa. Scott Olson/Getty Images hide caption

Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.

Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.

NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.
There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here.

If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.

articles.title: Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief
paragraphs: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., speaks at a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee hearing in Washington on Sept. 21, 2022. Samuel Corum/Getty Images hide caption
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled.

U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing.

There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.

Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached.

Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week.

For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats.
"What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked.

articles.title: Huw Edwards gives first interviews since child abuse image conviction
paragraphs: Disgraced former BBC News presenter Huw Edwards has given his first interviews since being convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children.
Edwards is seen saying he believes "silence is toxic" in a clip of a podcast released by the Observer newspaper, and he has also been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary.

A government minister, Anna Turley, told LBC, external she was "deeply uncomfortable" with the interviews, and that "for too long, so many of these people in the public eye have been able to have a sort of free pass".

Channel 4 has defended the documentary. A spokesperson told the BBC that a "highly experienced director" holds Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".
Edwards, formerly the BBC's most senior news presenter, pleaded guilty in July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and was given a suspended six-month prison sentence.
During the court case, Edwards admitted having 41 images, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.
In a trailer for the Channel 4 programme, director Patrick Forbes asks what he was doing, to which Edwards replies: "Oh, you want me to analyse what I was doing? I mean, seriously?"
The interviewer challenges him by saying: "Well, come on," to which Edwards angrily replies: "No, not come on."

articles.title: Veruschka: Striking images of one of the world's first supermodels, who has died aged 87
paragraphs: Veruschka was a distinctive presence on the covers of magazines like Vogue and Life in the 1960s and 70s
Veruschka, the model and artist who became one of the first global fashion stars in the 1960s, has died at the age of 87.
She became known as the striking subject of fantastical photoshoots that helped expand the boundaries of fashion and beauty in the 60s and 70s, appearing on the cover of American Vogue 13 times.

Vogue's obituary, external described her as "the shape-shifting supermodel who defined an era", explaining: "One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion's great performance artists."
She also made memorable appearances in classic swinging 60s film Blow Up and 2006 James Bond movie Casino Royale.
Veruschka was born Vera von Lehndorff into an aristocratic family in 1939 in Königsberg, then in Germany, now known as Kaliningrad in Russia.
Her father, Heinrich Count von Lehndorff, was executed in 1944 for his part in a failed plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler.
She studied art in Hamburg and Florence before beginning her career as a model "and soon became a legend", her sister Countess Catharina von Lehndorff wrote in a tribute, external.

articles.title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
paragraphs: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.
"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.
They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.

In the lawsuit, Pitt, 62, argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.
The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.
"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.

Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".
The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.

articles.title: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage
paragraphs: The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.
The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.
Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".
But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.
The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.
A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts
Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app
More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters

articles.title: Asha Bhosle and S. Janaki Remembered by Singer K.S. Chithra and Suhasini Maniratnam at IFFI’s Lata Mangeshkar Talk
paragraphs: Asha Bhosle and S. Janaki, two of Indian cinema’s most celebrated playback singers, were remembered at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa by singer K.S. Chithra and actor-filmmaker Suhasini Maniratnam.

Bhosle, a two-time Grammy nominee whose name was referenced in Cornershop’s 1997 hit “Brimful of Asha,” died in April at 92. Janaki, known as the Nightingale of South India, died in July at 88. Chithra and Suhasini shared their memories of the two at the annual “Lata Mangeshkar Talk: The Voice That Echoes Forever,” named for Bhosle’s elder sister, the singer Lata Mangeshkar. Related Stories ‘SNL’: Druski Dons Whiteface as Elizabeth Holmes in ‘You Can See Everything’ Parody ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Brutally Roasts Elon Musk Over 'Epic’ Midterms Defeat

Chithra, who has recorded more than 25,000 songs in several Indian languages over a career spanning nearly five decades, spoke about the singers who shaped her musical sensibilities, among them Mangeshkar, P. Susheela and Janaki. She imitated Janaki as a child, while acknowledging that the veteran singer’s distinctive style was impossible to reproduce. Mangeshkar’s devotional songs, she said, had particularly impressed her with their emotional depth.

Suhasini recalled an episode from the making of “Iruvar” (1997), directed by her husband Mani Ratnam. Composer A.R. Rahman, an Oscar winner for “Slumdog Millionaire,” had invited Bhosle to record a song that needed to evoke the style of Tamil playback singer L.R. Eswari, but was unsure how to explain the reference to her. He asked Suhasini to help. She demonstrated Eswari’s style, and Bhosle went on to deliver “Venilla Venilla.”

Chithra spoke about Bhosle’s versatility and her ability to move between musical forms, including ghazals, and about her desire to establish her own musical identity rather than be compared with her sister. At their first meeting, Chithra said, Bhosle asked her why she was singing in such a high register.

Janaki, Suhasini said, could inhabit a character through her voice, singing like a child or a teenage boy. Chithra recalled that Janaki was a devoted fan of Mangeshkar. She would play Mangeshkar’s songs on the radio, turn down the volume during the vocal portions and record herself singing along – “like a karaoke on her own,” as Chithra described it. Offstage, Chithra said, Janaki would feed her by hand when she visited her home.
The session also touched on the demands of recording and on recognizing one’s vocal limitations with age.

Chithra sang snippets throughout, including songs from her own repertoire and numbers popularized by Janaki and Bhosle. In a closing quiz, film clips were played without their background scores and Chithra was asked to identify each song by singing it. She identified all five.

articles.title: Jesse Plemons on the ‘Honor’ of Playing Plutarch in ‘The Hunger Games’ After Philip Seymour Hoffman and Debating Director Francis Lawrence Over the Character’s Motivations
paragraphs: “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” might be Haymitch Abernathy’s prequel movie, but Oscar nominee Jesse Plemons was the first person cast in the film.

Plemons plays Plutarch Heavensbee, a Capitol insider, who becomes a key figure in the rebellion that sparks in the latter half of Suzanne Collins’ original trilogy of dystopian novels. In the second book, “Catching Fire,” and its 2013 film adaptation, Plutarch is introduced as the Head Gamemaker, tasked with creating the brutal trials in the Hunger Games. (The late Philip Seymour Hoffman originated the role.) At the end of that story, Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) learns that Plutarch was really scheming from inside the establishment to help support the rebels. Related Stories Elon Musk Criticizes Jeremy Culhane’s ‘SNL’ Impression: ‘They Need to Try Harder’ ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Brutally Roasts Elon Musk Over 'Epic’ Midterms Defeat
But “Sunrise on the Reaping” takes place 25 years before those events, so casting the younger Plutarch was key.
“I’m a huge fan of Jesse’s,” franchise director Francis Lawrence tells Variety. “Had never worked with him before, and had always wanted to, and thought he would be perfect.”

Plemons, of course, is one of the blockbuster movie’s most accomplished stars — one of the star-studded ensemble’s seven Oscar nominees: Jennifer Lawrence and Kieran Culkin are winners, with Glenn Close receiving an honorary Oscar earlier this month.

“We had a lot of fun casting all these people fans are familiar with for this movie. But with [Plutarch] specifically, there was a lot more development,” Lawrence adds, sharing that he and “Hunger Games” producer Nina Jacobson spent considerable time working with Collins on Plutarch’s arc.

“He’s an infiltrator,” Lawrence explains. “He’s the guy at the beginning of the formation of the resistance, and at the same time, has to get to the place where by ‘Catching Fire’ he’s at Snow’s side and so trusted. So, it was on us to figure out how to portray Plutarch in a way that is believable. And that was fun because we were adding scenes that weren’t in the book.”

Book readers might’ve noticed a new Plutarch scene in the “Sunrise on the Reaping” movie — where Plemons appears bruised and bloodied after being brutally interrogated by President Snow (Ralph Fiennes), who’s learned of a secret plot to sabotage the 50th Hunger Games.

articles.title: John Travolta Didn’t Recognize Himself as Alleged JFK Assassin Johnny Roselli in ‘November 1963’: ‘I Went, “Oh My God, He’s the Devil”’
paragraphs: John Travolta rarely connects with all his characters. Sometimes, he even loves to hate them.

“They say you have to find something you like,” the actor explains. “But I’ve never felt that. I think you have to like the result, pulling it off. That’s where the joy comes from. To become these people, you don’t have to identify with them or enjoy being them. You just have to be excellent at executing them.” Related Stories James Talarico Crashes ‘SNL’ Cold Open: ‘I’m the Guy Who’s Been Texting You Every Day Asking for $5’ Bowen Yang Returns to ‘SNL’ as Jensen Huang as John Mulaney’s Cold Open Mocks Nvidia Scandal, National Ground Stop and Outlook Outage

Even so, Travolta faced one of the biggest challenges of his career playing a rather literal executioner in Roland Joffé’s “November 1963,” which opened the Torino Film Festival with its international premiere.

On paper, Johnny Roselli seems right in Travolta’s wheelhouse: a real-life wiseguy turned showbiz fixer, an Al Capone protégé whose career took him from Hollywood to Las Vegas to the Bay of Pigs, leaving a trail of bodies along the way.

“He was an odd mix,” says Travolta. “He was the guy who asked Sinatra to connect Kennedy with the mob. He hooked Kennedy up with Marilyn Monroe. He was a Hollywood icon of sorts, and had this other, darker side as a hitman. That’s complex. I’ve done dark subject matter before, but this was real. It actually happened, and that’s the difference.”

Roselli was purportedly a CIA go-between and sharpshooter. “November 1963” takes that history a step further, imagining him as a key triggerman on the Grassy Knoll, directly responsible for the killing that shook a nine-year-old boy in Englewood, New Jersey, and still haunts the actor to this day.

“It was the biggest crime of the century,” says Travolta, instantly transported back to second grade. “The announcement came at 11 a.m. Eastern Standard Time that the President had been shot, and then three hours later, at 2 p.m., they confirmed that he had passed. We all went to our homes, and all I can remember is being home with my father, glued to the television, sitting on his lap and trying to make sense of it all.”
Travolta carried that weight onto the set, where, he says, he was asked “to play a very evil man with moments of humanity.”

articles.title: Chiwetel Ejiofor on How Stephen Frears’ ‘Dirty Pretty Things’ Led Him to Fall in Love With Film
paragraphs: Chiwetel Ejiofor started his film career by doing something that many would consider as the absolute peak: he made a film with Steven Spielberg.
“Amistad” was his very first film and, understandably, he was afraid of peaking too soon.

“I was definitely worried about it at the time,” he said at Torino Film Festival. Related Stories Bowen Yang Returns to ‘SNL’ as Jensen Huang as John Mulaney’s Cold Open Mocks Nvidia Scandal, National Ground Stop and Outlook Outage John Mulaney Mocks Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in ‘SNL’ Monologue: ‘No One Likes Him. You Dumbass … Your Thing Can’t Be the Measles!’

“You feel that there are stages to how you develop as an actor and the opportunities you get, and you think they might follow a very linear path. But of course, my first film role was with Steven Spielberg. I realized then, very early on, that it’s a deeply unpredictable profession. You can either feel disquiet or anxiety about that, or you have to go with it.”

He added: “The opportunities can be sporadic or come from different places and angles that you didn’t imagine. Part of the challenge, but also the exciting thing about being an actor, is having the capacity and ability to roll with it, to travel on the journey of it and see where it takes you.”
The British actor came to Italy to receive the Stella della Mole award for lifetime achievement.
He admitted that, for the longest time, he didn’t see himself as a film actor.

“Even though I had done the Steven Spielberg film, I still thought of myself primarily as a theater actor. I worked with the National Theatre in Great Britain, in the West End and with many off-West End theater companies,” he said. In 2008, he won the Laurence Olivier Award for best actor for “Othello.”

articles.title: Luca Guadagnino Wants Next Movie to Be a ‘Love Story,’ Confirms ‘American Psycho’ and ‘Separate Rooms’ Not Happening
paragraphs: Speaking to Variety at the Marrakech Film Festival where he’s presenting “Artificial,” the Italian filmmaker behind “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All” and “Queer” revealed that he hopes his next directorial endeavor will be another love story.

“I think a lot of inspiration could come from facts of history,” Guadagnino said when asked what he would like to explore in his next film. “I want to make another love story, so I have to think about it, but I want to make a kind movie, another love story.” Related Stories Elon Musk Criticizes Jeremy Culhane’s ‘SNL’ Impression: ‘They Need to Try Harder’ ‘SNL’ Sets Timothée Chalamet and Robert De Niro as Final Hosts of 2026

“I want to make another love story, a kind movie,” Luca Guadagnino said at #MarrakechFilmFestival.However, the Italian director confirmed that the queer romance “Separate Rooms,” originally set to star Josh O’Connor, is no longer in the works. Guadagnino also addressed the… pic.twitter.com/kTmz3PlAZr

He also confirmed that two of his previously announced projects — a new adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’ “American Psycho” and the gay romance “Separate Rooms” — are no longer moving forward with him.

“Separate Rooms” was set to be an adaptation of Italian writer Pier Vittorio Tondelli’s 1989 novel about a writer grappling with the death of his lover. Josh O’Connor, who previously worked with Guadagnino on “Challengers,” and Léa Seydoux had been linked to the project since 2024.
“I don’t think I’m doing a movie with Léa Seydoux, unfortunately. That’s not happening,” Guadagnino said. “But I would love to work with Léa, of course.”

The director also addressed the demise of his “American Psycho” adaptation, which was first announced by Lionsgate in October 2024. The film, penned by Scott Z. Burns, was intended to be a fresh interpretation of Ellis’ 1991 novel rather than a remake of Mary Harron’s 2000 cult classic starring Christian Bale. “That’s the job of a director,” he said of its dissolution. “You direct movies and sometimes it happens, sometimes it doesn’t. It’s very simple and linear and usual.”

The filmmaker also dispelled speculation that Robert Pattinson had been in contention to play Patrick Bateman, though he said “he’s a perfect choice for James Bond,” adding: “He’s an incredible star, he’s done so many great roles and I wish someday to work with him, of course.”

articles.title: What’s New on Netflix for December 2026
paragraphs: Winter is here, and December is the perfect time to get cozy and hunker down for the holidays. What better way to do so than surfing the streaming platforms for a new show to binge or movie to obsess over?

“La Bola Negra,” which has garnered significant attention in its festival run, is one of the anticipated films joining Netflix this month. It follows the late-2010s historian tasked with connecting the pieces between a gay-themed Federico García Lorca play he inherits with the two other plot threads, including a narrative about the tender, illicit relationship between two soldiers on opposing sides of the Spanish Civil War (Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau). Related Stories Elon Musk Criticizes Jeremy Culhane’s ‘SNL’ Impression: ‘They Need to Try Harder’ ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Brutally Roasts Elon Musk Over 'Epic’ Midterms Defeat
Another anticipated title is the “Pride and Prejudice” TV series reboot exploring the deep relationship between Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy in a faithful yet fresh adaptation of the classic novel.
There are also several new holiday films like “The December Breeze” and “In a Holidaze.”
From box office surprises, to festive fun, Netflix has a slew of titles joining the platform this month.
“Gabby’s Dollhouse: Makers and Bakers Holiday”
“FIFA Women’s World Cup 2027 Final Draw”
“My Next Guest Needs No Introduction With David Letterman” Season 7

articles.title: Fury 'never received' schizophrenia diagnosis
paragraphs: Tyson Fury revealed his schizophrenia diagnosis in a new Netflix documentary
Paris Fury, the wife of Tyson Fury, says the boxer has never received a diagnosis of schizophrenia.

In clips promoting the release of a forthcoming Netflix documentary, the heavyweight fighter spoke of his mental health struggles in the months after he beat Wladimir Klitschko to become world champion in 2015.
He detailed hearing voices in his head, while wife Paris said he had "mild schizophrenia" .
Netflix has now edited the film ahead of its release on Friday, 27 November.
In a statement, Paris Fury said: "I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary.

"I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson's condition and I used the word 'schizophrenic'. While Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn't have this condition and has never received a diagnosis."

She added: "Mental health is complex, and it isn't always easy to find the right words, especially when you're living it with someone you love. I'm so proud of Tyson for really opening up in this documentary and want to say thank you for all the support we've received as a family."

articles.title: Bournemouth 'allowed to dream' as fans book Europa League final hotels
paragraphs: Marco Rose replaced Andoni Iraola - who ended up at Liverpool - in the summer
Bournemouth are dreaming of winning the Europa League after staging a 10-man fightback to join a select band of teams to win their first five European games.
The Cherries trailed 1-0 to Iago Aspas' goal at Celta Vigo, and then went down to 10 men midway through the first half when Bafode Diakite was sent off.
But second-half goals from Alvaro Rodriguez and Rayan gave the Cherries a 10th consecutive win in all competitions, extending their club record run.
Bournemouth are only the third side to win each of their first five European matches (excluding qualifiers and including the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup), after Nuremberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73.
They top this season's table as the only club to win five out of five - and are closing in on a top-eight spot, which would mean they skip a play-off round and go straight into the last 16.
Some fans have told the BBC they have already booked hotels in Frankfurt for the final on 26 May.
As supporters sang about reaching that game, midfielder Alex Scott was asked for his thoughts on TNT Sports.

articles.title: India's Pant joins New Zealand club match under false name
paragraphs: India wicketkeeper Rishabh Pant made a surprise appearance for a club team in Christchurch under the false name 'Stan Stan'.
Pant, 29, played for the Open House Swingers against The Chosen Ones and smashed 54 from 21 balls in a 16-run win.
His appearance came a day before India's second Test against New Zealand, which begins at the Hagley Oval at 22:00 GMT on Thursday.
Open House player Mohammad Safi told the New Zealand Herald that he had seen Pant on an electric bike in the city and approached him, saying that his team were a player short.
Safi also said that Pant was not immediately recognised by many on either side, and he turned up in a purple tracksuit and had to borrow kit.

New Zealand captain Tom Latham said Pant's appearance was "brilliant" and showed his "real character", while India bowling coach and former South Africa quick Morne Morkel said he "nearly fell off my chair" when he saw the footage that circulated on social media.
The first Test in Wellington ended in a high-scoring draw, where Pant scored 128 in India's only innings of 720-9.
Pant is regarded as one of the world's most entertaining cricketers, and has scored 3,853 runs in his 53 Tests at an average just shy of 45.

articles.title: No post-match drug testing in South Africa v New Zealand series
paragraphs: The Springboks and All Blacks played three Tests in South Africa before a fourth in the American city of Baltimore
South Africa and New Zealand players were not subjected to a single post-match drugs test by anti-doping authorities when they contested this year's Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.
The four-Test series, played in August and September, is a new biennial initiative between the two southern hemisphere powerhouses aimed at boosted revenues and profiles.
An agreement over how the series operates refers to World Rugby anti-doping rules; but, in practice, post-match tests, which are standard practice at most elite-level matches, were not carried out.
Players in the series could have been tested by either of two official bodies.
All players involved in the series are part of World Rugby's testing pool. The global governing body conducts on-the-spot tests on top players around the world throughout the year.
The South African Institute for Drug-Free Sport (Saids) runs its own domestic anti-doping programme, covering sporting events and athletes in the country.
With all matches, bar the fourth and final Test in the American city of Baltimore, taking place in South Africa, Saids could have demanded samples from players after games.

articles.title: Taylor and Lewis lose all five pairs matches on return
paragraphs: Phil Taylor won a record 87 major titles before retiring after losing the 2018 PDC World Darts Championship final to Rob Cross
Phil Taylor and his England team-mate Adrian Lewis lost all five matches as the pair returned to darts action together at the MODUS Super Series International Pairs tournament.
Taylor, a 16-time world champion, retired from senior-level darts in 2018, while Lewis has not competed on the PDC tour since 2023.
They signed for the tournament in Portsmouth after Taylor was tempted back by the prospect of playing alongside his long-term friend.
The 66-year-old landed his first dart at a double as he checked out on 84 but the duo went on to lose their opening match 4-3 against Scotland's John Henderson and Robert Thornton.
They subsequently suffered successive defeats to pairs from Sweden, Switzerland, Germany and Denmark.
The pair finished the night bottom of Group C, but will return to action on Friday for a second round-robin phase.
Taylor had not played competitively since the 2024 edition of World Seniors Darts Championship and was adamant the south-coast competition will be his last appearance at the tournament.

articles.title: Russell says Verstappen's criticism 'quite amusing'
paragraphs: Russell and Verstappen have had several rows during the past few years
George Russell has said Max Verstappen can "say what he wants" and explained he found the Red Bull driver's criticisms of him after the Las Vegas Grand Prix "quite amusing".
Verstappen said Russell was "so far below my level" after winning the race on Saturday.
His remarks were a response to Mercedes driver Russell saying "somebody has to stand up to this guy" after an on-track confrontation in practice.

Russell said before this weekend's penultimate grand prix of the season in Qatar: "I stand by what I said after practice, but he was the one who went out and won the race and I didn't, and I'm sure he had a bit of a laugh about that and it was reasonably amusing.
"He drove an incredible race and won it and he can afford to say what he wants."
Russell v Verstappen: F1’s New Rivalry Explodes in Vegas
Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A
