articles.title: Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
paragraphs: More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.

About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals.
That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July.

In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.
Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years.
On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.
Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals.

articles.title: Simon Jack: Is Poundland's US owner to blame for its collapse?
paragraphs: The blame game for the demise of Poundland is in full swing.
The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for £1 and have taken nearly £20m out of the business already.

Gordon Brothers stand to get paid back a further £22.5m, as their share of an existing £30m loan is set to be one of the first debts that the administrators will have to pay out of the proceeds of any sale of the business in whole or in part.

The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period.
They point to improving sales over recent months as proof the business had a future.
MPs also laid into the US firm with members of the Business Committee accusing it of "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping".
No-one appears to dispute the fact that Gordon Brothers' insistence that they get paid most of their £22.5m debt was a major stumbling block to a sale.
Potential buyers balked at paying out millions on a loan that Gordon Brothers inherited for nothing.

articles.title: New boss appointed to lead Travelodge
paragraphs: Peter Krueger will lead Travelodge after a turbulent few months
Travelodge has appointed a former Tui executive to become its new boss from the start of December.
The former CEO of the Oxfordshire-based budget hotel chain Jo Boydell quit in the summer after safety issues were raised at many of its sites.

A woman staying at its Maidenhead hotel was sexually assaulted in December 2022 after a man lied to staff to get a key card to her room. Kyran Smith was jailed for seven-and-a-half years for the attack.
Peter Krueger will start his new role at Travelodge on Tuesday, replacing interim chief Ray Reidy who has led the company since Boydell quit.
She left the company after facing significant criticism over the handling of the sexual assault incident and wider safety concerns.
It prompted former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer to urge her to "seriously engage" with the government on the issue after she cancelled a meeting with MPs.
An independent review by Paul Greaney KC published in October found the sexual assault victim was treated in a "disgraceful" way and "fundamentally failed" by the hotel chain.

articles.title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
paragraphs: Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.
The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.
Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.
Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.
Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.
But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.
A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.

articles.title: Guitar wars - the transatlantic battle over the Stratocaster
paragraphs: The Fender Stratocaster is widely considered to be the best-known shape in electric guitars
Hans Thomann leads the way through his music store in central Germany to the large electric guitar department, where the walls are hung with hundreds of instruments.
Brands on show include famous names Fender and Gibson, plus Harley Benton.
The latter is a low-price range of guitars owned by the family-run company that Thomann leads – Thomann, one of the world's largest online retailers of musical instruments.
The shop, together with warehouses and offices, are at the company's headquarters in the tiny village of Treppendorf in rural Upper Franconia, in Bavaria.
The business was founded by Thomann's father, Hans Thomann Senior, in 1954.
In one corner of the store, a young man is trying out a Fender Stratocaster, one of the world's most iconic electric guitars.
Designed in the US in the early 1950's, the "Strat" became the instrument of choice for many famous rock and pop musicians, such as Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Buddy Holly.

articles.title: Semiconductor chips are the new oil. Here's why
paragraphs: The artificial intelligence boom has pushed semiconductors past oil and gas in global export value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data.

Yet the milestone arrives at an awkward moment, just as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and drive down the price of semiconductor stocks. Last week, before Monday's breathtaking reversal, semiconductor stocks suffered their worst weekly loss in a quarter century, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone, capping a more than 17% weekly decline.

Nvidia soared more than 31% Monday after the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips had fallen for a seventh straight week, plunging 46% during that stretch. Then it fell again, dropping almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 20% in two days last Thursday and Friday. Micron Technology sank 27% over the seven days ended last Friday.

"For decades we've talked about the petrodollar. Perhaps increasingly we need to think about the chip dollar," Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank wrote in a report this month.

Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time during the January-March quarter of 2026, reaching about $1.61 trillion, compared with $1.53 trillion for oil and gas, the report said, using four-quarter rolling totals.

The gap widened in the second quarter, when semiconductor exports totaled about $1.60 trillion and oil and gas exports reached about $1.47 trillion. Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz after the Iran war helped widen the gap. Daily oil flows through the Strait collapsed nearly 77%, to 4.9 million barrels in the second quarter of 2026 from 21.6 million barrels in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Yet the demand for semiconductors has proven insatiable in the face of soaring data center construction, boosting global trade in the increasingly scarce AI component. Hundreds of billions of dollars of orders for graphics processing units and data centers aim at providing AI computing power, Rothschild & Co. Redburn wrote in a report last Thursday.
"Compute will be the new commodity fueling this transformation on a global scale," Rothschild analyst Cara Thomson said.

articles.title: Buyer beware? Nvidia's volatile swings expose risks of single-stock ETFs
paragraphs: Nvidia's latest bout of volatility is highlighting risks tied to single-stock exchange-traded funds.

Among the hardest hit: the GraniteShares 2x Short NVDA Daily ETF (NVD). The fund sank 63% on Monday after Jensen Huang got reinstated as the chip giant's CEO. Meanwhile, the firm's 2x Long NVDA ETF (NVDL) soared nearly 62% on the same day.

ETF Action founding partner Mike Akins joined "ETF Edge" as Nvidia shares soared 31% during Monday's session, wiping a large portion of the losses from the days following Huang's resignation. Shares cooled on Tuesday and Wednesday, however.

"Historically speaking, we do not see these types of large drawdowns followed by huge drives up in a healthy market," Akins said on Monday. "It usually tends to be when you're in a recession or in a bear market territory, which we're not technically in for the broader market, but we are in for this AI trade."
But it may not be time to go cold turkey on single-stock funds.

"[Leveraged ETFs are] definitely a retail trading vehicle… I think it's OK to have a little fun trying to trade that," Akins added. "I'm certain there are people that are better at trading these than others. But on the whole, timing the market is very, very hard."

GraniteShares founder and CEO Will Rhind also joined "ETF Edge" on Monday as Nvidia single-stock short ETFs overshadowed his firm's new Anthropic launches: The 2x Short Anthropic Daily ETF (ANS) and the 2x Long Anthropic Daily ETF (AIL).

"We thought this was going to be the biggest news event of the day with Anthropic the first leveraged ETFs going live," he said. "I can tell you this is like a sideshow compared to what we're seeing with Nvidia."

articles.title: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike
paragraphs: In a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era?

Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution.

It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation, the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.
Bottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution.

It may be that the massive capex spending on AI will mean more productivity and less inflation down the road. But the front-end build-out is proving to be more inflationary, and more challenging, to a Fed already dealing with high inflation. In many ways, that's the opposite of what Greenspan had to handle.

articles.title: Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans
paragraphs: As Amanda Brecht planned how her family would spend Thanksgiving this year, she had to make some difficult decisions.

Because of high gas prices, the 30-year-old decided she wouldn't drive across her home state of Michigan to celebrate with extended family. Instead, Brecht and her husband will spend the holiday with just their three kids. And with food prices rising, they'll be skipping appetizers and serving turkey breast instead of a whole bird.
"Thanksgiving is definitely going to look different this year," Brecht said. "Money doesn't grow on trees. You can only do so much."

With inflation accelerating, Americans like Brecht will see higher prices almost everywhere they look this holiday season. At a time of year synonymous with food, gifts and big spending, many consumers are instead pinching pennies, paring back their plans and making tough choices about how they'll celebrate.

Some are raiding their savings accounts and running up debt on credit cards. They're reporting downbeat outlooks about the economy in surveys. And they've become more selective with spending as inflationary pressures mount.

"Families are facing some tough choices this year," said Alexander Smith, an associate professor who researches behavioral economics at the Worcester Polytechnic Institute. "They might have to cut back on holiday spending in whatever way that they can."
A classic Thanksgiving feast will be harder to pull off as grocery prices rise.

The price of a 10-person Thanksgiving dinner increased 6% to $58.63 in 2026, according to an annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation. Faith Parum, the organization's deputy chief economist, said the price increase was a result of higher costs for labor and transportation.

articles.title: Microdrama apps chase profits as Hollywood moves into short-form, vertical video
paragraphs: Bogdan Nesvit says his mission is simple: "We are essentially building Disney for the 21st century."

Nesvit is the co-founder of microseries app My Drama, built around the latest, bite-sized form of storytelling. Short, serialized "microdrama" videos are created specifically for mobile devices and have generated billions of views this year. They often feature romantic tropes and typically end in cliffhangers to keep viewers hooked.
The category has exploded at a time when traditional media faces waning interest and YouTube now claims more viewing hours than individual streaming platforms.

The microdrama industry is projected to reach $1.5 billion in revenue in the U.S. in 2026, according to research firm Media Partners Asia. In China, where the format originally gained popularity, microdrama revenue surpassed what was made at the box office in 2024.
"It has the potential to evolve into mainstream entertainment and basically become mobile-first video streaming of the size of Netflix," Nesvit said.
Tech companies and startups such as My Drama currently lead the category in metrics like downloads and time spent on the apps.
TikTok's PineDrama is the most popular microdrama app of 2026 so far with 13.2 million U.S. downloads through September, according to Sensor Tower data.
Startups DramaBox and ReelShort beat out entertainment giants Netflix and Disney in average mobile usage time in the U.S. in the third quarter, according to Sensor Tower.

articles.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
paragraphs: A small fossil discovered in Scotland and regarded for nearly three decades as one of the earliest known reptiles has turned out to be a very different kind of prehistoric animal. New research published in Nature is challenging its long-established place in evolutionary history. The study was led by scientists at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility.

The 345-million-year-old fossil, discovered in 1984, belongs to a species called Westlothiana lizziae. Nicknamed "Lizzie" because of its resemblance to a lizard, the specimen consists of a nearly complete skeleton preserved in two crushed slabs of rock. Early descriptions relied largely on anatomical features visible at the surface, including four limbs with fingers and toes that appeared to have claw-like tips. These characteristics distinguished Westlothiana from many other animals living at the time, whose limbs more closely resembled fins.

Although the fossil's distorted condition made its anatomy difficult to interpret, researchers widely regarded it as the earliest known amniote adapted to life on land. Amniotes are a major group of vertebrates that includes reptiles, birds, and mammals. Following its scientific description in 1990, Westlothiana became an important reference point for researchers investigating when and how these animals first evolved.

"Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades," said Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum's Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. "But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected."

Using powerful X-ray imaging technology at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, the scientists peered beneath the surface of the rock and reconstructed previously inaccessible parts of the animal's anatomy.

What they discovered was strikingly different from the anatomy expected in an early reptile. Lizzie possessed a primitive skull, internal gills containing bone, and a mouth resembling that of a fish, complete with thousands of tiny teeth. Together, these features rule out its previously proposed position within the evolutionary lineage leading to reptiles. Instead of living primarily on land, Westlothiana appears to have been an aquatic or amphibious animal.

"The surprisingly primitive features of the skull show us that Lizzie was not only not a reptile but belonged to a much more ancient lineage. It turns out looks can be deceiving, and Lizzie lived a completely different lifestyle than we previously thought," said Ben Igielman, co-lead author of the study, who started this research during his graduate work at the University of Oxford.
The discovery also changes how scientists understand the origins of several anatomical features traditionally associated with vertebrates adapted to terrestrial environments.

articles.title: The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men
paragraphs: Men and women appear to be similarly skilled at juggling multiple activities, but new research has uncovered one striking difference. In an experiment designed to recreate the demands of everyday life, men ignored conversational questions more than twice as often as women while performing just as well on the other tasks.

Whether driving, working, doing household chores, or enjoying leisure activities, people frequently find themselves managing several tasks at once or switching between them. Although women are widely believed to be better at multitasking than men, previous research has found only minor and inconsistent differences between the sexes, raising doubts about the accuracy of this popular assumption.

With support from the Bial Foundation, researchers André and Diana Szameitat (from Brunel University of London and City St George's, University of London, UK, respectively) set out to determine whether meaningful differences exist in multitasking ability and what might explain the widespread belief that women have an advantage.

In their study, "Men Talk Less Than Women During Multitasking," published in the scientific journal Psychological Research, the researchers developed an experiment involving five different activities. The setup was designed to capture the complexity of everyday multitasking more accurately than most previous studies.

The first experiment involved 41 men and 37 women. Participants were asked to follow a recipe in a kitchen setting, look up phone numbers, match numbers with letters, watch a slideshow for specific words, and answer conversational questions. A new question was posed every 20 seconds (e.g., "Would you rather lose all of your money and valuables or all of the pictures you have ever taken, and why?").

In a second experiment, the researchers recruited 160 observers to determine whether differences in multitasking behavior were noticeable to others. Without being given prior information about the participants or findings, the observers watched video recordings of the experiments and assessed how well the participants performed.

Men and women achieved comparable results on four of the five activities. Conversation, however, revealed a notable exception. Men left conversational questions unanswered more than twice as often as women. When men did answer, their responses were just as fast and of comparable quality to those given by women.

The researchers suggest that women may, on average, be more inclined to engage in communication during social interactions. However, the study did not directly investigate this possibility, so the explanation should be treated with caution. The results are also consistent with evolutionary theories suggesting that women may have a greater tendency to engage in conversation.

articles.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
paragraphs: More than a mile below the surface of the Red Sea, researchers from the University of Miami (UM) Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science discovered rare deep-sea brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern extension of the Red Sea. These unusually salty underwater lakes could provide clues to how Earth's oceans formed millions of years ago and help guide the search for life on other planets.

The discovery was made by Sam Purkis, professor and chair of the UM Department of Marine Geosciences, and his colleagues in collaboration with OceanX. The researchers located the pools at a depth of more than one mile (1,770 meters) using a remotely operated underwater vehicle (ROV) deployed from the OceanXplorer, an advanced research vessel equipped to investigate some of the least accessible environments on Earth.

"Until we understand the limits of life on Earth, it will be difficult to determine if alien planets can host any living beings," said Purkis. "Our discovery of a rich community of microbes that survive in extreme environments can help trace the limits of life on Earth and can be applied to the search for life elsewhere in our solar system and beyond."

Brine pools rank among the harshest environments on our planet. Their waters contain exceptionally high concentrations of salt, feature unusual chemical conditions, and are completely devoid of oxygen. Despite these seemingly inhospitable conditions, the pools support abundant microbial life. Previous research on microbes inhabiting Red Sea brine pools has even identified biologically active molecules with potential anticancer properties.
The findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, mark the first documented discovery of brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba. Remarkably, the researchers nearly missed them.
"We were very lucky," said Purkis. "The discovery came in the last five minutes of the ten-hour ROV dive that we could dedicate to this project."

Beyond their biological significance, the pools serve as natural archives of the region's geological history. Situated relatively close to the coastline, their extremely salty waters and absence of oxygen help preserve evidence of tsunamis, flash floods, and earthquakes that occurred in the Gulf of Aqaba thousands of years ago. Regional tectonic activity has produced numerous faults and fractures across the seabed in this part of the gulf.

Earlier in 2022, Purkis and his colleagues uncovered evidence of a 500-year-old underwater landslide that likely generated a substantial tsunami. Understanding the region's history of such events could have important implications for coastal development in Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong
paragraphs: Research has established that loneliness can have serious consequences for physical health. However, a new University of Michigan study warns that treating loneliness primarily as a health problem could shift responsibility away from society and place it on a healthcare system that lacks the tools to restore meaningful social connections.

Published in Social Problems, the study examines how chronic loneliness and social isolation became recognized as major public health concerns after researchers uncovered links to illness, premature death, and increased healthcare spending.

Previous studies highlighted in the research illustrate the severity of these consequences. One estimated that lacking social connections could be as harmful to health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Another found that loneliness, social isolation, and living alone were each associated with an approximately 30% higher risk of premature death. The financial burden is also substantial, with separate research estimating that social isolation costs Medicare $6.7 billion each year in care for older adults.

"Once people saw these findings, they began to treat loneliness as urgent," said University of Michigan doctoral student Sofia Hiltner. "But it made me wonder: Why do we only consider problems important once they are tied to health?"
To understand how loneliness became a medical concern, Hiltner conducted interviews with experts and reviewed more than a decade of media coverage, medical journal articles, and academic literature.

Her analysis revealed that establishing a connection between loneliness and poor health helped the issue gain credibility. However, it also encouraged what she describes as a "logical leap": the belief that any problem affecting human health should become the responsibility of the healthcare system.
"Not everything that relates to health belongs in healthcare," she said. "Doctors can screen patients and connect them to services, but they cannot rebuild communities or shorten work hours."

Hiltner, a predoctoral trainee in social demography at the Population Studies Center within the University of Michigan's Institute for Social Research, was inspired to investigate loneliness after witnessing her grandmother become increasingly isolated as she aged.

articles.title: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results
paragraphs: Robotic technology can help surgeons perform knee replacement operations with greater precision, but that accuracy does not necessarily translate into better results for patients. The RACER-Knee trial, the world's largest clinical study of its kind, found that patients who underwent robot-assisted knee replacement experienced similar levels of pain, mobility, and recovery to those who received conventional surgery. The findings provide important evidence about the use of robotics in health care and highlight where future technological developments and research could make a difference. Coordinated by the University of Warwick and University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust, the trial was published in The Lancet, the world's oldest and one of its best-known general medical journals.

Robotic technology is becoming increasingly common in knee replacement surgery around the world. It is now used in 6% of procedures in the UK, 16% in the US, and 42% in Australia. The technology is designed to help surgeons position artificial knee joints more accurately and customize procedures to suit each patient's anatomy.

The UK-wide RACER-Knee trial was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) in partnership with Stryker, the manufacturer of the robotic equipment evaluated in the study. The Warwick Clinical Trials Unit, UHCW NHS Trust, and the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital in Birmingham led the research. It represents the world's largest double-blinded, randomized controlled trial comparing traditional total knee replacement with procedures performed using the Stryker Mako robotic system, the most widely used system of its kind worldwide.

Twelve months after surgery, patients in both groups reported comparable recovery, mobility, and pain levels. Although the robotic system enabled surgeons to operate with greater precision, patients did not experience measurable improvements in their overall outcomes during the first year. The researchers also found no increased risk of serious adverse events associated with robotic assistance, suggesting that it was as safe as conventional surgery.
The trial was jointly led by two chief investigators in the UK.

Professor Andrew Metcalfe, of Warwick Medical School at the University of Warwick and a consultant orthopedic surgeon at UHCW NHS Trust, said: "We are delighted to have completed this world-leading randomized trial of an exciting technology that is now being used globally and at scale. It is an important step in the process of innovation and will stimulate lots more high-quality studies. We are very grateful for the support of the many patients who took part which is so important, but also the NIHR and Stryker for working so well together to support this critical study. Technology such as this could really help the care we give for patients, but for robotic-assisted knee replacements, there is still work to do before we see benefits such as less pain or better movement."

Professor Edward Davis, a consultant orthopedic surgeon at The Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and honorary professor at the University of Birmingham, said: "The trial demonstrates robotic-arm-assistance allows for higher precision, and in theory the system should allow surgeons to customize the procedure according to a patient's anatomy. These results are by no means a condemnation of the robotic systems, but more understanding of the ideal position for a knee replacement and personalization for each patient is needed. We'll then be able to truly take advantage of the advanced precision of robotic systems."

Professor Anthony Gordon, director of the NIHR Health Technology Assessment (HTA) Programme, said: "Innovation in healthcare depends on evaluating promising technologies rigorously and at scale. While this study shows robotic-assisted knee replacement is not yet improving patient outcomes, it highlights opportunities to refine these technologies and harness their precision to deliver better care in the future. The NIHR continues to fund robust studies, such as RACER, ensuring we learn how to deliver the latest technologies most effectively within the NHS."

articles.title: Floating nature islands installed in parks as Glasgow Games legacy
paragraphs: Volunteers from local communities have been involved in setting out the plants
Floating islands are being installed on ponds in five of Glasgow's parks as part of the 2026 Commonwealth Games legacy.
The islands, which are being planted by community groups, are designed to encourage wildlife and help clean the water.
The project will create almost 250 square metres of new wildlife habitat which is expected to last about 20 years.
Glasgow 2026 organisers say they are funding the projects as part of their commitment to greener games.
Ellen Hebdon says the plants' roots play an important role in preventing and removing harmful algae from the water
The islands are manufactured by a Moray-based company which has been exporting them around the world.
Biomatrix Water Solutions in Forres has installed islands in Boston, Venice and London.

articles.title: Watch: Man and dog narrowly escape powerful king tide in Oregon
paragraphs: Footage from Cannon Beach, Oregon, shows a man and a dog being swept away after a powerful wave surged ashore during unusually high "king tides".
Both the man and his dog escaped unharmed, the police department said.
Authorities have urged people to stay away from beaches as record-breaking tides, large waves and coastal flooding affect parts of the US west coast.

articles.title: Second court defeat for Trump's deep-sea mining ambitions
paragraphs: Campaigners worried the mining could impact sea turtles in the area

The Trump administration's plans to begin deep-sea mining in the Pacific have hit a second legal setback after a federal judge ruled plans to lease areas of sea-floor off the Northern Mariana Islands violated the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The court's decision follows a similar ruling over a proposed lease sale off American Samoa.
Opposition groups who lodged the Northern Mariana Islands lawsuit said they were concerned deep-sea mining could cause long-term damage to the ocean ecosystem.
The US government has said it wants to start deep-sea mining to enable access to critical minerals and to counter China's growing influence over crucial components needed for electronics.
The administration had planned to put up for sale leases for the Northern Mariana Islands on 16 December 2026.

It is not clear what will happen next as the administration chose not to recognise the first court ruling and went ahead with the sale of two leases covering 13 million hectares (more than 30 million acres) off American Samoa.

Ruling on the Northern Mariana Islands case, District judge Jill Aiko Otake said the defendants, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), which provided the expert opinion behind the lease sales, and Howard Lutnick, who was named in his capacity as head of the department that oversees the agency, had failed to consider the potential effects that could follow once the leases were issued.

articles.title: More than 1,000 flights cancelled or delayed in US as weather disrupts Thanksgiving travel
paragraphs: Powerful storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North America
Nearly 400 flights in the US have been cancelled so far on Thursday as bad weather coincides with busy travel on the Thanksgiving holiday.
Another 1,200 flights into, out of, or within the US have been delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.

On Wednesday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) briefly grounded all flights heading for Miami International Airport after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway. No injuries were reported, and the FAA is investigating.

More than 80 million Americans were expected to be traveling this week at the same time the National Weather Service (NWS) has forecast storms along the western and eastern coasts of the US that could bring heavy rain and flooding.
FedEx aircraft sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway

The FAA previously warned that delays across the country would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast. On Wednesday, FlightAware reported more than 6,800 delays and more than 160 cancellations.
The NWS forecast a strong storm will deluge the eastern US coast on Thursday, bringing high winds, heavy rainfall and major coastal flooding.

articles.title: US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
paragraphs: Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation site

The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the controlled detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa: an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.

Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Wednesday following the detonation around the ammunition plant, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".
An all-clear was issued. Local soil, air and water continue to be tested.
Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.
In an update late on Wednesday, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin said air monitors were detecting zero airborne lead after the controlled explosion.

He wrote on X that the agency would "continue to be radically transparent with the public as sample results come in from the laboratory", and that these were "projected to start arriving back over the next 24 to 48 hours".
His post added: "Our goal is to complete ALL sampling by tomorrow and will remain on the ground to complete any remediation if at all necessary."

articles.title: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa
paragraphs: Lenacapavir has received WHO's approval for HIV prevention

Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.
Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.
The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.
The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.
Focus on Africa podcast: Lenacapavir offering new hope for HIV prevention?

articles.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
paragraphs: S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

articles.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
paragraphs: While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.
Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.
Jagmeet covers startups, tech policy-related updates, and all other major tech-centric developments from India for TechCrunch. He previously worked as a principal correspondent at NDTV.
The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America Kirsten Korosec
Figma employee sues, alleging company forced her to confront harassers Dominic-Madori Davis
Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes Sarah Perez

articles.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
paragraphs: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”

The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”

Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”

Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
paragraphs: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”

“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”
Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”

articles.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
paragraphs: Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffs
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.

The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.

articles.title: Images of asteroid targeted to test Earth's defences reveal stadium-sized crater
paragraphs: The asteroid before (left) and after, showing the crater left behind by a spacecraft's impact
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.
Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.
"The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team.
"It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."
The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

articles.title: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
paragraphs: Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.

Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.
Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.

The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.
It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.

articles.title: Israeli judges recommend dropping most serious charges against Netanyahu
paragraphs: Benjamin Netanyahu called for his trial to be ended "immediately"
Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.

The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.
They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.
Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".
"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.
"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."
Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.

articles.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
paragraphs: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.

The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower.
The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks.
Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day.
Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.
The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.
Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.
The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

articles.title: Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
paragraphs: As dawn broke one recent morning over camp, we got one of our first full views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, normally hidden behind clouds.

Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts. The beating sun bakes you during the day, walking so close to the equator, but the nights quickly dip below freezing. Snow remains constantly in sight from humid rainforest and alpine landscapes, freshly charred from a wildfire three weeks before. And always beckoning is the peak, within sight, but seemingly never nearer; the high altitude means hikers need to walk slowly or else risk exhaustion and altitude sickness.

A group of friends and fellow hikers and I spent days camping at altitude to acclimatize before a final summit push during our second-to-last evening on the mountain. We trudged through heavy snow under the stars, cresting a massive volcanic crater rim, and leaned against drifts of what had become a full blizzard to reach the top in the early morning hours. I stood on the peak I'd seen only from a distance for the last week but saw only whiteness: all snow and ice, the absence of life and color heightened by my low oxygen levels.

Days later, having descended and decompressed and readying myself to fly back home, I looked back at the mountain one last time. For a few minutes, in the dusk light, the clouds parted and she revealed herself before disappearing again into the darkening evening, still as elusive as ever.

articles.title: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
paragraphs: FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.
A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.
The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.

The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.

"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."

articles.title: Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco
paragraphs: FILE - Senegal's Sadio Mane holds the trophy aloft as he celebrates with teammates after winning the Africa Cup of Nations final soccer match between Senegal and Morocco in Rabat, Morocco, Sunday, Jan. 18, 2026. Youssef Loulidi/AP hide caption
More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.
Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.
Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.
CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.
"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.
The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.

Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."

articles.title: Gordon Ramsay to host Top Gear as show revived after Flintoff crash
paragraphs: 'Top Gear is back': Gordon Ramsay announced as new host
TV chef Gordon Ramsay is to lead the new presenting line-up on BBC motoring show Top Gear, which is being revived four years after it was last on air.
Ramsay will take the driving seat alongside as yet unnamed co-presenters when the show starts filming next year. It will return to screens in 2028.

The long-running programme has been off air since 2022, when co-host Andrew Flintoff suffered serious facial and rib injuries after his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned at the show's test-track.

In a statement announcing his new role, Ramsay said he wants to bring "a fresh energy and ambition" to the show's formula of being "surprising, entertaining and [with] just the right amount of chaos".
Andrew Flintoff, Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris hosted the show before it was rested
Top Gear began in 1977 and became one of the BBC's biggest hits in the hands of Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May in the 2000s.
They were replaced by hosts including Chris Evans and Friends star Matt LeBlanc, before Flintoff took over in 2018 with Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris.

articles.title: Hundreds complain about I'm A Celebrity after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu 'aggressive'
paragraphs: AJ Odudu said being called aggressive was "very harsh" and it was "an insane word" to use about her

More than 800 people have complained to the media regulator about an episode of ITV reality show I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! in which Mariella Frostrup accused her campmate AJ Odudu of being "aggressive".
Ofcom said 887 people had filed complaints about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu.
An Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."

The pair were seen clearing the air on Tuesday, with broadcaster Frostrup saying she was "sorry for calling you aggressive" and Odudu telling her it is "a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".
Wayne Rooney tried to repair relations between AJ Odudu (left) and Mariella Frostrup on Sunday
Relations between the pair became fractious when Odudu attempted to help Frostrup cook on Saturday's episode.
Tensions flared further as they and other campmates discussed their friction and the cooking arrangements the following morning.

articles.title: Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a true Wild Boy
paragraphs: Andy Taylor, who has died aged 65, was the wild boy of Duran Duran.
In the early 1980s, the pop legends sold over 100 million records and dominated the charts in both Britain and the United States.
But success came at a cost. For Taylor, global superstardom became a cocaine and alcohol fuelled nightmare that left him burnt out and battling clinical depression.
"For sure, we paraded around in our fast cars with beautiful models on yachts in the south of France without needing to pay the bill," he later wrote.
Andrew Taylor was born in North Tyneside on 16 February 1961.
Home was Cullercoats, a coastal village near Whitley Bay where many people, including his uncles, depended on the sea for their livelihoods.
At first, it was a happy childhood. There was church on Sunday with his parents, Ronnie and Blanche, followed by games of football on the beach with younger brother Ronnie junior.
On Christmas Day, his extended family would belt out Bing Crosby hits around the piano.

articles.title: BBC appeals against decision to allow Trump's $10bn lawsuit to go ahead
paragraphs: The BBC has lodged an "urgent" appeal against a US judge's decision to allow Donald Trump's $10bn (£7.6bn) lawsuit against the corporation to go ahead.
The US president is suing the BBC for defamation over the way an episode of Panorama edited a speech he gave in January 2021, shortly before the riot at the US Capitol.
Earlier this month, a federal judge in Florida ruled that the defamation case could proceed after the BBC sought to dismiss it.

The BBC has now filed an appeal with a higher court, saying there is a "complete lack of evidence" that anyone in Florida accessed the programme, and that the broadcaster made "rigorous and systematic efforts to prevent access to the documentary" in the US.
A BBC spokesman said: "We are surprised and disappointed by the court's decision that this case should be heard in Florida.
"As we have made clear from the start, the BBC broadcast this documentary in the UK - and UK only. We did not show it in Florida, nor did any other broadcaster.
"Given the urgency of this issue, we are now requesting a higher court review the ruling."
President Trump's lawsuit accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave on 6 January 2021.

articles.title: Bake Off winner crowned after high-stakes final
paragraphs: (From left) Moyin Odeniran, Mo Mahir and Tom Whittaker all made Tuesday night's final
Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Great British Bake Off final
Moyin Odeniran said he was "in shock" after being crowned the winner of the 17th series of The Great British Bake Off.
The 22-year-old from Loughton, Essex, described it as a "very busy time" as he juggled competing in the Channel 4 baking competition with completing his university studies.
Despite his dissertation being due a month after filming wrapped, Odeniran achieved a first in his political economy degree at King's College London.
He beat fellow finalists Tom Whittaker, from West Yorkshire, and Birmingham student Mo Mahir to the title in Tuesday night's episode.
"I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here. I can't believe it – I am in shock," the talented baker said.
"I have made friends for life and I have just loved every single second of it, and I don't think I could have asked for anything more."

articles.title: NBC Plans to Give Thanksgiving Parade Ads Extra Run After Macy’s Postponement
paragraphs: NBC has a Thanksgiving Week present for advertisers scheduled to appear in the now-postponed Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

The network plans to run commercials from sponsors of the event twice this week — once when the 2026 parade airs on Saturday and once on Thursday, when the network will run a repeat of last year’s Macy’s extravaganza. In short, Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade advertisers get two runs on the network for ther price of one. The details were confirmed by an NBC spokesperson. Related Stories Sofia Coppola Pays Tribute to Late Mother Eleanor Coppola at Paris Screening of ‘Making Marie Antoinette’ Hosted by Chanel and Mubi 'Hyena,' Thriller Exec Produced by David Lynch, to Star Kiernan Shipka, D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai, Edgar Ramírez and Rosemarie DeWitt

Macy’s and NBC decided to postpone the parade to Saturday, November 28, citing extreme wind conditions and inclement weather expected on Thursday. Many of the signature balloons used in the parade cannot be controlled properly during high wind speeds. The network said it is “committed to ensuring this remains a high-priority opportunity for our clients with both the reach and scale of tomorrow’s re-airing and the original live telecast on Saturday.”

NBC has many reasons to keep advertisers in the parade happy. The cost of a 30-second commercial in the parade is up 15% to 20% over last year, according to Guideline, a tracker of ad spending, when NBC was able to charge between $900,000 and $1 million per unit. Those figures would indicate that a 30-second spot in the 2026 parade could cost between$1.03 million and $1.2 million. Ad spend on the event is pacing about 25% to 30% ahead of last year, according to Guideline. The parade snared more than $88.7 million in ads last year, the company says.

The parade is also part of a time-honored lineup that includes the National Dog Show and a primetime NFL game. The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade telecast was the opening event in a extended schedule of holiday programs that the network uses to lure marketers eager to court holiday shoppers.

Geico had plans to run a two-minute commercial that uses stop-motion animation featuring many of its trademark characters, such as the Geico Gecko. Starbucks had signed on to promote a new holiday album, “The Holiday Blend,” and is the sponsor of a takeover of an NBC livestream of the parade on TikTok.

NBC isn’t the first TV network to confront delays tied to a massive live event. CBS in 2013 gave some of the advertisers in that year’s Super Bowl an extra run of their commercials after a 35-minute power outage brought a game between the Baltimore Ravens and the San Francisco 49’ers. Bud Light and Subway were among the marketers that enjoyed an extra airing of ads that had multi-million-dollar price tags.

articles.title: ‘The Hawk’ Starring Will Ferrell Canceled After One Season at Netflix
paragraphs: “The Hawk” has hit the rough. Netflix has canceled the golf comedy series after just one season.

The series, which starred Will Ferrell in his first regular TV role since “SNL,” originally debuted on the streamer back in July. While the show did make it into the Netflix global top 10 chart for three weeks upon its release, the cost of the series, which sources say was increased by Ferrell’s salary as star and co-creator, raised the bar for success that would have led to a second season. Related Stories 'Hyena,' Thriller Exec Produced by David Lynch, to Star Kiernan Shipka, D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai, Edgar Ramírez and Rosemarie DeWitt Sofia Coppola Pays Tribute to Late Mother Eleanor Coppola at Paris Screening of ‘Making Marie Antoinette’ Hosted by Chanel and Mubi

The official logline for “The Hawk” states “Lonnie Hawkins (Ferrell) ,2004’s number one golfer, struggles on the back nine of his career to recapture his magic. His body says retire, but his heart says he’s not done yet. His ex-wife and his son Lance, golf’s new golden boy, know he’s through. But with one more major to win to complete golf’s Grand Slam, Lonnie refuses to believe he’s anything other than one stroke away from the greatest comeback in golf history.”
Along with Ferrell, the cast included Molly Shannon, Jimmy Tatro, Fortune Feimster, Luke Wilson, Chris Parnell, Katelyn Tarver and David Hornsby.

Ferrell co-created the series with Harper Steele and Chris Hency. All three were executive producers along with Jessica Elbaum and Alix Taylor for Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions; Rian Johnson, Ram Bergman and Nena Rodrigue for T-Street; David Gordon Green; and Andrew Guest.

While this was Ferrell’s first starring role in a Netflix show, he has produced a number of series at the streamer over the past several years and has multiple projects in the pipeline. He is executive producing new series “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and Nikki Glaser’s first scripted series as part of her Netflix Is a Joke Studios deal, all via Gloria Sanchez Productions.

articles.title: Tony Romo, After Parting Ways With CBS Sports, Named ‘Chief Predictions Officer’ of Jake Paul’s Betr Betting App
paragraphs: Former NFL quarterback and football analyst Tony Romo has landed his next gig: He’s joined Betr, the sports gambling app co-founded by Jake Paul, as its first-ever “chief predictions officer.”

In the new role, Romo will serve as “a prominent face of the Betr brand,” appearing in original content, delivering sports predictions and engaging with fans across the company’s gaming products, including Picks, Predictions, Social Sportsbook, Social Casino, Arcade and Rips. As part of the agreement, Romo will become an equity stakeholder in Betr. Related Stories Peacock Is $2.99 a Month With This Black Friday Deal ‘Gugu’s World’ Team on the Diversity of Brazilian Cinema and Championing Films That ‘Respect the Storyteller’

Romo, former QB for the Dallas Cowboys, had been an on-air analyst with CBS Sports since 2017. Last month, the network announced it was parting ways with Romo. That came after Romo had pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated stemming from an incident that took place in Milwaukee in July.

Romo said: “I’ve spent my entire career trying to anticipate what’s going to happen next, whether that was on the field or in the broadcast booth. Now I get to put those instincts to work in a completely new way with Betr.” He added, “I’m looking forward to having some fun, making predictions and being part of where this company is headed. And I’ve got a pretty good feeling about what’s coming next.”

“Tony Romo has built an extraordinary reputation around something that sits at the very heart of our business: predictions,” Joey Levy, founder and CEO of Betr, said in a statement. “His ability to see what’s coming before anyone else has made him one of the most compelling personalities in sports, and we see a tremendous opportunity to bring that talent and personality to our growing ecosystem.”
Romo joins Betr’s roster of sports and entertainment talent partners, including NBA veteran Patrick Beverley, former Heisman Trophy winner Johnny Manziel and actors Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier.

articles.title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Season 35 Finale Attracts 9.2 Million Viewers
paragraphs: “Dancing With the Stars” aired its Season 35 finale live coast-to-coast for the first time on Tuesday, and the results were big. A season-best 9.2 million total viewers watched Paralympic track and field athlete Ezra Frech and partner Daniella Karagach take home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, according to Nielsen live+same-day preliminary, panel-only program ratings.

According to ABC, the finale posted a 2.38 rating with adults 18-49, which made it the best number in the demo since Nov. 25, 2014 (coincidentally, the season when now-host Alfonso Ribeiro won the trophy with partner Witney Carson). The finale was also up 11% in the demo vs. last year’s telecast (2.15 rating). Related Stories Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed to Saturday Due to Storm 'The Hawk' Starring Will Ferrell Canceled After One Season at Netflix

That 2.38 rating makes it TV’s top entertainment telecast with adults 18-49 since the Oscars in March and the highest-rated regularly scheduled entertainment telecast in 18-49 since the April 1, 2020, episode of Fox’s “The Masked Singer.”
In total viewers, the 9.2 million viewers matched last year’s finale.

In other demos, the finale averaged a 2.86 rating with adults 18-34 — the best performance since the Season 12 finale on May 24, 2011. With women 18-34, “Dancing With the Stars” posted a 4.46 rating, which is the best series telecast number in the demo for any network broadcast since the Season 3 premiere of Fox’s “Empire” on Sept. 21, 2016. And the show posted the best teens 12-17 rating (1.18) since “The Masked Singer” on Feb. 27, 2019.

ABC said the finale attracted more than 86 million votes, a new high (up 19% from 72 million in 2025) — the most ever for a single episode. The finale was the No. 1 most social program on television across broadcast and cable on the night and the No. 1 most social episode of any broadcast primetime series, year-to-date.

“Dancing with the Stars” aired live in every U.S. time zone for its special three-hour finale on Tuesday; the finale also re-aired in primetime in the Pacific time zone and started streaming the next day on Hulu.
The five final couples also included Amber Glenn and partner Pasha Pashkov, Maura Higgins and partner Mark Ballas, Connor Wood and partner Rylee Arnold and Tatyana Ali and partner Jan Ravnik.

articles.title: New ‘Rocky’ Book Celebrates 50th Anniversary With Rare and Never-Seen-Before Paintings
paragraphs: Sylvester Stallone‘s classic film “Rocky” premiered half a century ago.
To mark the occasion, artist John Rivoli has released a new book, “The Fine Art Of Rocky: An Artistic Tribute From Screen To Canvas,” published by Insight Editions.

The book features rare and never-before-seen original Rocky paintings by Rivoli, an official MGM/Amazon Rocky artist. Related Stories ‘Steven Universe’ Star Zyri Comes Out as Trans Hollywood Gets Roasted in Satirical Picture Book ‘We Make a Movie’: ‘I Loved Your Script … Now Change Everything’ (EXCLUSIVE)

Part art book and part analysis of the six Rocky films, the book invites fans to revisit the iconic franchise through Rivoli’s collection of large-scale original paintings and iconic posters, seeing the beloved character in a whole new light.

Rocky takes center stage in this deluxe book, with over 70 of Rivoli’s paintings, posters and other unique artworks highlighting unforgettable moments from the films presented in original and unique perspectives as well as art collaborations with Stallone.
Rivoli said, “This book represents a lifetime of training — for this moment, for this story, for this opportunity to reinterpret Rocky through my own artistic lens.”

Speaking with Variety, Rivoli pointed to two pieces featured in the book. The first, “Alone in the Ring,” is something that holds a special place in his heart. “I struggled with how to tell this story visually. I knew that to capture the true significance of the moment, I had to make Rocky small on the canvas. As an artist, that’s a difficult decision when you know collectors want a large, commanding image of Rocky hanging on their walls.”

Rivoli says the painting wasn’t about making Rocky larger than life. “It was about showing him surrounded by something much bigger than himself. The ring is enormous, the arena is vast, and the towering image of Apollo Creed dominates the space. Everything around Rocky is larger than he is, emphasizing just how small and alone he feels in that moment.”

articles.title: Andy Taylor, Duran Duran Guitarist, Dies at 65
paragraphs: Guitarist Andy Taylor, whose tenure in England’s glammy, pop-savvy rock band Duran Duran coincided with the group’s commercial pinnacle of the early ‘80s, died of prostate cancer at his home on Monday while surrounded by family. He was 65.

In a statement shared with Variety, Taylor’s wife Tracey said on behalf of their family, “To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather. He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.” Related Stories Generative AI Indian Feature 'Maharaja in Denims,' Inspired by Sikh Ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Sets April 2027 Release (EXCLUSIVE) Veruschka, Supermodel Who Appeared in 'Blow-Up,' 'Casino Royale,' Dies at 87

Duran Duran added, “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”

Taylor, who was diagnosed with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, had opted out on appearing at the group’s November 2022 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, citing a decline in his health in a statement.

He said, “Although my current condition is not immediately life-threatening there is no cure…. Recently I was doing OK after some very sophisticated life-extending treatment, that was until a week or so ago when I suffered a setback, and despite the exceptional efforts of my team, I had to be honest in that both physically and mentally, I would be pushing my boundaries.”

Duran Duran had been in existence for two years in the Midlands city of Birmingham when Taylor — then a 19-year-old Northumberland native seeking new opportunities after successfully touring British army bases in Europe with cover bands — spotted a April 1980 Melody Maker classified ad seeking a “Live Wire Guitarist.”

He wrote in “Wild Boy,” his candid and frequently sensational 2008 autobiography, “[The ad] cited Mick Ronson of the Spiders From Mars and Steve Jones of the Sex Pistols as musical influences so I thought it looked worth a call.”

After a successful audition, Taylor became a member of the quintet, which became a popular fixture at the Birmingham club the Rum Runner. Sporting extravagant coiffs and makeup — “We’d end up discussing cosmetics with the girls,” Taylor later wrote — the band was lumped in with Britain’s New Romantic movement of the early ‘80s. After only eight months with Taylor in the lineup, the act was signed by EMI.

articles.title: Dubois to defend title against Parker in Manchester
paragraphs: Daniel Dubois and Joseph Parker were first due to fight in February 2025
WBO heavyweight world champion Daniel Dubois will make the second defence of his title against former WBO champion Joseph Parker next year at Co-op Live in Manchester on 30 January.
The pair were set to meet in February 2025, but Dubois, then the IBF title holder, was forced to withdraw through illness in fight week.
New Zealand's Parker has not fought since his provisional doping suspension was lifted in August.
"This heavyweight showdown will deliver a blockbuster beginning to 2027," boxing promoter Frank Warren said.
"It's a fight everyone wanted to see, and I'm thrilled we can now make it happen. Daniel is entering his prime and, when he is on his game, it is hard to picture anybody beating him.
"But Joseph has long promised to become world champion again, and now he gets his chance."
Parker, 34, was defeated by Fabio Wardley in his last bout in October 2025 - the same opponent that Dubois has beaten in his past two fights.

articles.title: Regulator chief 'has stomach' to face Man City
paragraphs: Manchester City are currently third in the Premier League
The chair of English football's independent regulator has told MPs he "has the stomach" to take potential action against Manchester City.
The club was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-season period by an independent commission.

The verdict, published in September, found City's Abu Dhabi owners - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president Sheikh Mansour - inflated revenues and disguised losses by £900 million through "sham" arrangements.
