City deny wronging and have appealed, but if the ruling is upheld, they could face an investigation by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).
It has the power to remove directors if they are deemed unsuitable, and even to force a sale of the club.

Appearing in front of parliament's Digital, Culture, Media and Sport select committee, IFR chairman David Kogan was clear that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate the club's hierarchy and take action, if deemed necessary.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," he said.

articles.title: Sterling - from England icon to suspended jail sentence
paragraphs: Raheem Sterling has scored 123 goals in 396 Premier League appearances and provided 65 assists
Raheem Sterling grew up a stone's throw from Wembley Stadium, and went on to start a European Championship final for England there.
At his peak, the four-time Premier League winner was earning £325,000 a week at Chelsea.
"Raheem is a huge player with a huge influence in the last few years in English football," said then Blues boss Thomas Tuchel when he signed a 27-year-old Sterling in a £50m deal in 2022.
"He is at the perfect age to take responsibility around the younger players that we have and be an example.
"He just needs to do what he did over the last few years and he will be a huge asset for us."
Sterling enjoyed a 10-year England career, also played for Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal, and commanded combined transfer fees of about £100m.

But his career at the top level looks to be in the balance at the age of 31 after he was handed a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, for dangerous driving. Sterling has also been disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.

articles.title: Glasner criticises Forest players yet to learn English
paragraphs: Nottingham Forest have suffered successive 2-0 defeats on the road to Brentford and Bournemouth

Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner says standards at the club were not good enough when he arrived, and has questioned why some of his squad cannot speak English after being in the country for a number of years.
Forest are one place above the relegation zone heading into Friday's home game against Chelsea, winning just two of their first 11 games in the Premier League.
"Stability in a company is having standards," said Glasner. "Everybody who joins commits to the standards. I think, very honestly, the standards were not high enough.
"We have players who are here for four years, can't speak English. If you go to Italy, after three months, every player gives his interview in the Italian language.
"For me, if I want to manage in England, I have to speak English. If I want to manage in Italy, I have to speak Italian.
"Otherwise, Oliver Glasner, if you want to speak in your dialect, stay at home in Austria, everybody understands you, but nowhere else."

Forest, who narrowly avoided relegation last season but who did reach the Europa League semi-finals, have had a succession of managers in recent years and while Glasner refused to blame the upheaval for any problems he has inherited, he feels standards need to rise.

articles.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
paragraphs: Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.

The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.
Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached.
Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret".

He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.
"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added.
Kelvin Blake, pictured at a protest in Walsall, has worked for Poundland for 25 years

Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere.

articles.title: What's gone wrong at Poundland?
paragraphs: The future of Poundland hangs in the balance after the discount retailer's collapse into administration.
Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.
Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.
Its collapse puts the jobs of its 11,000 employees at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.
People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.
Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.
According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor, "this isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland".

articles.title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge
paragraphs: Watch: Martin Lewis' tips on staying warm this winter
Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although the price will depend on how much energy a household uses, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter.

A household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit, would see their annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if the increase was sustained for a year, said regulator Ofgem.
The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.
Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

Ofgem said the rise had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war. Wholesale gas prices, paid by suppliers, were up 33% in the last three months, the period used to set the January to March cap. They have more than doubled since late 2025.
The warm home discount will take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.

articles.title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
paragraphs: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.
"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.
In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.
In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16, external. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.
Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.
In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.
"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.

articles.title: Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation
paragraphs: Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche told him Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation.

"I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters in Ohio on Wednesday after being asked what assurances he had gotten that Huang was not under investigation. "Not even that he was about to be prosecuted; that he's under no investigation."
Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done.
Trump was asked what Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws.
"They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said Monday.
Reuters reported Wednesday that the Department of Justice did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his reinstatement as CEO.
Blanche had concluded there was no evidence Huang had broken any laws based on investigations into Nvidia clients Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed, according to the report.

The DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Reuters report. And the White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Vance saying Huang was under no investigation when Trump had said there was one. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about Vance's remarks.

articles.title: SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1 million orbital data center satellites
paragraphs: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.
Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

The FCC, in its authorization filing, noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC (Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."
In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."

The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."
The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr, who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.

Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher, which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.

articles.title: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving Day Parade due to severe weather
paragraphs: Macy's on Wednesday announced it's postponing its Thanksgiving Day Parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, due to severe weather.

The parade, held each year on Thanksgiving morning, will now take place on Saturday at 8:30 a.m. ET, according to the company. The New York City area is expected to have heavy rain and thunderstorms on Thanksgiving.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement.
This year's event marks the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The annual event has never been canceled due to weather, though it was suspended between 1942 and 1944 for World War II.

The parade's viability this year had been in question after concerns arose over strong winds that could become dangerous for the massive balloons that the event is known for. Many of the balloons had already been inflated as of Wednesday afternoon.
The postponement also means thousands of volunteers and artists slated to perform will have to adapt to Saturday's schedule.

articles.title: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
paragraphs: The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies, including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce.

The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March, weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities.

The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.

The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties.

The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning.
"In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer said. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points."

An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the new tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer said. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action."

The senior U.S. official said Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said.

articles.title: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, raising the 2027 stakes for the central bank
paragraphs: Inflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in the cards for December and raising questions about how much more work the central bank will have to do in 2027.

The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual inflation rate, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly twice the central bank's goal. The reading was 0.1 percentage point higher than September.
Excluding food and energy, core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. That was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast.
While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends.

A separate report also showed much stronger economic growth for the third quarter, with gross domestic product rising at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate. The strong top-line gain for the economy adds further fuel to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not restricting economic activity.

Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, which matched the pace of price increases but was 0.1 percentage point lower than forecast. Income, on the other hand, surged 0.7%, much more than the 0.4% estimate. The personal saving rate rose to 4.1%.

Stock market futures added to losses following the release, while Treasury yields also were sharply lower. Even with the higher-than-expected core inflation figure, expectations eased a bit for Fed rate hikes in 2027. Traders continued to price in two more increases but lowered odds for a third hike to about 1-in-3, compared to 50-50 on Tuesday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch.
"Inflation is too hot and it will not be brought under control as long as economic demand is also too hot," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds.

articles.title: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains
paragraphs: Adults age 65 and older who have dementia or other cognitive disorders are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of medications used to treat anxiety, sleep disturbances, psychosis, and other conditions affecting the central nervous system.
Potential consequences include more emergency room visits, longer and more frequent hospital stays, declining mental health, and an increased risk of premature death.

New research from the University at Buffalo (UB) offers some encouraging news, however. Between 2011 and 2022, the proportion of older adults with cognitive disorders taking medications that could impair their cognitive function decreased significantly.

After analyzing data from 2,796 older adults with cognitive disorders who lived independently, researchers found that exposure to potentially inappropriate medications fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022.

"This is a population with some mental issues that relate to the central nervous system. These drugs also act on the central nervous system, so they can be too much for older adults if inappropriately used," says Haowen Hsu, PharmD, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Pharmacy Practice at the School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences and first author of the study, published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society.

Older adults who have spent years taking benzodiazepines such as Xanax for anxiety or sleep medications such as Ambien may benefit from a medically supervised reduction in dosage or gradual discontinuation. These medications can negatively affect cognitive function, balance, and coordination.

"A central word for patients in this age group is 'deprescribing,' which means, for example, removing inappropriate medications and decreasing the frequency or the dosage. In some cases, it means replacing the current medication with a milder alternative," Hsu says. "This is why it's so important for health care providers to work closely with community pharmacists and homecare nurses to optimize medication safety."

To identify potentially problematic drugs, the research team consulted the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, which identifies approximately 100 medications that may pose risks to older adults. The researchers then concentrated specifically on medications that could present additional dangers for people with diagnosed cognitive disorders.

articles.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
paragraphs: The European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid space telescope has made an unexpected discovery in our own solar system. Images captured between September 16 and 24, 2026, revealed a previously unknown comet, the first discovered by the mission.

The achievement is particularly remarkable given that Euclid was built to capture detailed images of distant galaxies rather than track rapidly moving objects such as comets. The speed with which researchers identified and confirmed the discovery demonstrates that Euclid can detect new comets while they are still relatively far from the Sun. This capability could eventually help identify a target for ESA's upcoming Comet Interceptor mission.

Mikko Pöntinen, a PhD student at the University of Helsinki, made the discovery with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium. Pöntinen developed specialized software to detect and track small solar system objects appearing in the telescope's images.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images -- the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas."

The object appeared in a region of the sky known as the 'Euclid Deep Field North'. Over several days, the telescope captured it in five separate fields of view, taking between two and four exposures of each field for a total of 16 exposures.

After searching catalogs of known asteroids and comets without finding a match, Pöntinen submitted the observations to the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center (MPC) as a potential new comet. The report enabled astronomers using telescopes on Earth to carry out additional observations. On October 8, the MPC officially confirmed the discovery. The comet has been designated C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

The newly discovered comet is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers (about 800 million miles) from Earth. That distance is comparable to the distance from the Sun to a point somewhere between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

However, the comet is traveling well outside the relatively flat plane in which the planets orbit the Sun. It is currently positioned almost directly above the Sun, following a sweeping path over the solar system that will take thousands of years to complete.

articles.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
paragraphs: Physicists at Northwestern University have achieved an unprecedented level of quantum control over a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists answer one of the most fundamental questions in physics: Why does the universe exist as we know it?

The researchers captured a rapidly moving positron produced through radioactive decay, slowed it down, and cooled it to a temperature just above absolute zero. They then confined the particle within a near-perfect vacuum, isolating it from ordinary matter, which would cause it to annihilate.

Using this approach, the team created what they call a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." Within this system, the positron behaves somewhat like an artificial atom, allowing researchers to observe and precisely manipulate its individual quantum energy levels.

The achievement lays the groundwork for what could become the most rigorous test yet of the fundamental symmetry between electrons and positrons. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that the two particles should behave as nearly perfect mirror images of each other.

By measuring the positron's magnetic properties with unprecedented accuracy and comparing them with those of an electron, scientists could uncover previously undetected differences. Any unexpected discrepancy would point to a weakness in the Standard Model and potentially offer clues to why the universe contains so much more matter than antimatter.

"Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction," said Northwestern's Gerald Gabrielse, who led the study. "If you take an electron and an anti-electron (or positron) and collide them together, they both disappear. We describe that as annihilation, a concept that fuels science fiction writers' imaginations. The big mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we'd be left with nothing. There's clearly something wrong with that theory, and that's what we're trying to figure out."

Gabrielse is the Board of Trustees Professor of Physics at Northwestern's Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and director of the university's Center for Fundamental Physics. Thomas Myers, a Ph.D. student working in Gabrielse's laboratory, is the study's first author.

The Standard Model is one of the most successful theories in modern science. It describes the universe's fundamental particles and three of its four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces). Countless experiments have verified its predictions with remarkable accuracy.

articles.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
paragraphs: A new Stanford Medicine-led study has identified three distinct biological brain types, known as biotypes, in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety disorder or both conditions.

The findings could help unravel the complicated relationship between two of the most common childhood mental health disorders, which frequently share symptoms. Published recently in Nature Mental Health, the study reveals that each biotype involves disruptions in a different set of brain circuits.

By examining thousands of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three biological patterns associated with different groups of symptoms. These findings could eventually help doctors recognize ADHD and anxiety earlier, identify new targets for treatment, and determine which therapies are most likely to benefit individual patients.

"The high overlap between ADHD and anxiety actually hinders our understanding of the neurobiology underlying traditional, symptom-based diagnoses," said co-senior study author Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences.

Doctors currently rely on symptom checklists to diagnose ADHD and anxiety. However, Zhang explained that children diagnosed with either disorder frequently experience symptoms associated with the other.

Yong Jiao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Iowa, is the study's lead author. Zhang shares senior authorship with Jing Jiang, PhD, assistant professor of pediatric neurology at the University of Iowa.
"We wanted to know whether the biological differences among children with ADHD and anxiety follow the diagnostic labels used in the clinic," Zhang said.

The researchers found that the relationship was not so straightforward. Children diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety or both could belong to any of the three brain biotypes, although some biological patterns were more prevalent among children with particular diagnoses.

articles.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
paragraphs: The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory. Researchers propose that the brain not only communicates through electrical signals but may also "write" and "read" memories through chemical interactions involving neurons, astrocytes, and the molecules surrounding them. By linking memory to emotion and thought, the theory raises an increasingly relevant question: Can computational power alone give rise to the kind of consciousness experienced by living organisms?

Hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades. A distinctive scent can bring a forgotten person or place to mind, while recalling a terrifying experience can trigger both emotional and physical reactions within moments.
Like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information. However, the mechanisms underlying biological memory may be fundamentally different.

A new review by Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Professor Chaim Gilon of the Department of Chemistry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem explores the physical and chemical mechanisms that could link memory, emotion, and thought.

In their paper, "Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective," the researchers suggest that understanding memory requires more than studying neurons and their electrical activity. They argue that other brain cells, particularly astrocytes, and the intricate molecular environment surrounding them may also play essential roles.

Building on their previous research into the molecular foundations of memory, Marx and Gilon examine whether the processes responsible for storing and retrieving experiences could also shed light on the origins of intelligence, thought, and consciousness.
Central to the researchers' proposal is a model known as the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory.

According to this theory, memories emerge from interactions between three major components: brain cells, especially astrocytes working alongside neurons; the molecular substances surrounding those cells; and various chemicals, including metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

articles.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
paragraphs: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a new study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

"In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," said first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship."

Since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

"Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," said Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions."

articles.title: Canadian astronaut welcomes baby girl from space station
paragraphs: A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.
Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday.
"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency.
Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.
The couple have two older children, aged five and seven.
"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."
In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true.

"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.

articles.title: New York's annual Thanksgiving Parade threatened by approaching storm
paragraphs: The sun shone on 2025's Thanksgiving Parade but the forecast this year is not so bright
Strong winds are threatening to disrupt Thursday's Thanksgiving parade in New York City for the first time since World War Two.

A potent Nor'easter storm could impact the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade which is due to be taking place for the 100th time, with the risk that it could be too windy for the event's iconic balloons to fly.

The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade is due to end.
Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern USA as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow.
Western areas of the country have also faced Thanksgiving travel headaches, with Pacific storms and coastal flooding.
Storms targeting both US coasts threaten to snarl Thanksgiving travel for millions
The parade started life as the Macy's Christmas Parade, organised by employees at Macy's department store in New York City in a bid to boost holiday sales.

articles.title: Why has China sent the first Pakistani astronaut to space?
paragraphs: China has sent a Pakistani astronaut along with two Chinese astronauts onto its Shenzhou-24 mission, marking the first time a foreign national has set foot aboard the Tiangong space station.
The landmark moment for 40-year-old air force pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali highlights China's desire for its space station to become an international research facility.
The mission is expected to last for several days before returning to Earth.

articles.title: China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut into space
paragraphs: Historic space mission lifts off with first Pakistani astronaut aboard Chinese rocket

China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.
Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".
The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".
While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.
The mission comprises of payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, flight engineer Wu Yi and commander Tang Hongbo
They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.

articles.title: NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement
paragraphs: How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace.

NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

“We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”

Under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

“Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”
Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

“GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” said Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”
NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.

articles.title: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus
paragraphs: As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.
Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

But looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.

articles.title: Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard
paragraphs: Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

“I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

“I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

She began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.
When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

“Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she said, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”

articles.title: Eye of the Sahara
paragraphs: The Richat Structure, also known as the “Eye of the Sahara,” is seen from the International Space Station as it orbited above on Nov. 14, 2026. It is an eroded geological dome about 100 million years old created by igneous activity and uplift in the nation of Mauritania. In this type of geologic structure, rocks exposed in the center of the “bullseye” are older than rocks forming the outer rings. This structure measures 45 kilometers (28 miles) across and is made up of igneous and sedimentary rocks.

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble Views Ocean of Stars in Groundwork for Roman
paragraphs: An expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way. The images focus on an area of sky toward the galactic bulge, a densely packed, spherical region of stars that surrounds the center of a galaxy’s disk. These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.

Astronomers study the Milky Way’s galactic bulge because it holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s stellar mass, and its proximity allows them to examine the region in greater detail. Although we can see the glow from these crowded spheres of stars in other galaxies, they are too jam-packed and far away to resolve individual stars. By studying the Milky Way’s galactic bulge, researchers hope to find new planets and better understand how galaxies form, evolve, and interact over billions of years.

Hubble views the universe primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light, while Roman collects data in near-infrared light and some visible light. Because researchers wish to compare Hubble’s observations to future Roman observations, Hubble looked at the region in wavelengths that overlap with Roman’s areas of sensitivity, the red end of the visible spectrum and near-infrared wavelengths.

Hubble’s high resolution allows its instruments to collect data on the brightness, ages, composition, and motion of stars over time. With this knowledge, astronomers can search for potential exoplanets, determine the location of black holes or dark matter, and better understand our galaxy’s environment and evolution.

A key component of Roman’s future observations is the search for exoplanets by capturing microlensing events, a type of gravitational lensing that occurs when light from a more distant object is magnified and distorted by the mass of a closer object along the line of sight. The way light from the distant star is distorted and magnified can reveal clues to the nature of the foreground star and any planets it may have. Hubble's observations will help characterize stars in the region before they undergo a lensing event. Months or years in the future, when Roman captures a microlensing event, researchers can compare Hubble data to Roman data of the event, making it easer to interpret. These microlensing events are on a much smaller scale, that of stars and planets, than larger gravitational lenses that occur around galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Over Hubble’s lifetime, it has observed our galaxy’s central bulge many times. These legacy surveys include the WFC3 Galactic Bulge Treasury Program that used Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 to study the brightness, precise positions, and motions of stars in this congested part of our galaxy. It also includes the Sagittarius Window Eclipsing Extrasolar Planet Search (SWEEPS) that used Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys to look at 180,000 stars in the bulge of our galaxy. These new observations come from an observing program (#17776: S. Terry) designed to aid Roman in its search for exoplanets, black holes, neutron stars, and more. The data also adds to Hubble’s continuing legacy of high-precision observations of stars in the galactic bulge.
Claire AndreoliNASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MDclaire.andreoli@nasa.gov
Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.

articles.title: APOD: 2026 November 25 – SPHEREx Seeing Through Dust
paragraphs: Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Explanation: What is blocking the center of the Milky Way? During its 13 billion years, our Milky Way has collected a lot of dust. In contrast to the skin cells, dirt, pollen, and other debris that make up the dust behind your couch, cosmic dust is hundreds of times smaller and made of tiny compounds of oxygen, carbon, and other elements released into space when a star dies. Today’s video shows infrared light from the Milky Way’s center gathered by NASA’s SPHEREx satellite. Each false color in the video corresponds to the infrared color associated with the wavelength shown in the top left. In the near-infrared, like 1.2 microns, light gets absorbed and scatters off of dust particles. SPHEREx then sees the Galactic Center almost entirely blocked by clouds of dust. In the mid-infrared, though, light is able to pierce through the dust and reach SPHEREx. This is similar to, but not exactly, why sunsets are red!Tomorrow's picture: a sandy view of the Milky Way

articles.title: Third of young Brits have never had sex, but many are sexting and watching porn
paragraphs: British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study reveals.
It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' (Natsal, external) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours.
Half of people aged 16 to 24 have sent or received sexual images on their phone in the last year, while one in two young women and almost nine in 10 young men say they have viewed pornography.
But a third of this age group have never had sex, up from a fifth in the last study 12 years ago.
Adults under 45 are having less sex too, doing it twice a month, on average, down from once a week in 1990.
More than one in three (37%) women said they had watched porn in the past year.
Among the 16-24 year-olds, half of women and most young men (86%) said they watched it.

Porn use and masturbation were less common among people who had never had sex, which the authors say suggests solo and online activity is not simply replacing in-person sex, although they cannot be sure.

articles.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
paragraphs: Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas.

Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.
The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.

Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.

“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”

When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”

When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics.

The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero‘s AI Puppy.

articles.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
paragraphs: What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.

Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)

Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.

In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.

articles.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
paragraphs: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

articles.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
paragraphs: How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

articles.title: French ex-President Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to face trial
paragraphs: Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.
The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.
Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.
In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.

In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.

The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.
Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.

articles.title: Indian government has 'lost the plot', says 'cockroach' leader barred from UK flight
paragraphs: Watch: India's government is 'scared', cockroach movement leader says after travel ban
One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK.
Saurav Das said he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth.

In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people.
The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared".

"They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them."
By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world.

articles.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
paragraphs: Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which also included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

articles.title: Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war
paragraphs: Syrians coming back after the war are falling victim to mines and other explosives
Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.
"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.
Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.

The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).
The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.
Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.
But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

articles.title: Nigerian monarch, 92, suspended after sexual assault claims
paragraphs: Umar Farouk Umar has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother, who reigned for 41 years
One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.
The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.
The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.
Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.

He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.

Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.
Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.

articles.title: Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?
paragraphs: The sun sets over coastal mountains near the city of Vlore, the region where Jared Kushner plans to build a five-star luxury resort. The land that Kushner bought for this project, though, is claimed by several local Albanians and its ownership is being investigated by state prosecutors. Rob Schmitz/NPR hide caption

ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.
And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.

"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."

A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."

Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.

Gentian Mocka says his family has owned this strip of beach, named Hidrovor Beach, since the time of the Ottoman Empire. The land is now slated to be developed for a luxury hotel owned by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump. In the background is Sazan Island, a publicly owned island that Trump and Kushner also say they will develop. Rob Schmitz/NPR hide caption

"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.

articles.title: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia. And, Rep. Gomez resigns amid alleged sexual misconduct
paragraphs: Your support helps make our show possible and unlocks access to our sponsor-free feed.

Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO yesterday, causing the company's stock to soar more than 30%. President Trump claimed credit for facilitating Huang's return. The CEO's comeback follows his resignation just two weeks earlier due to reports of extramarital affairs, including involvement with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, a close ally of the president, had previously donated $25 million to the new White House ballroom and security complex. His return boosted Nvidia's stock and triggered a rally in the entire stock market, revealing that one man's comeback is worth about a trillion dollars. Some individuals advocating for diversity and inclusion in Silicon Valley argue that Huang's return signals that profit is the only priority.

Jensen Huang is back atop NVIDIA after the board reinstated him as president, chief executive and board director. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in a statement. Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe hide caption

Ukraine recently sank a Russian warship in Libya, while Russian missiles struck Poland. There has been no comment from the Kremlin on the strikes. Depending on perspective, Russia's war in Ukraine appears to be either escalating or de-escalating. This month, the Trump administration said it is making progress towards a negotiated peace. However, fighting has expanded into Eastern and Northern Europe and the Mediterranean.

Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., has announced his resignation from Congress following a bipartisan investigation that found "substantial evidence" of his alleged sexual misconduct toward a House staffer. The House Ethics Committee determined that Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances" and disregarding the power imbalance in his relationship with staff. The report says his actions could amount to criminal sexual assault. Gomez, who has represented parts of Los Angeles since 2017, lost his reelection bid this fall to Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. Gomez says he has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.

Maryana Cavalcanti do Nascimento de Oliveira plays timpani (kettledrums) at the Baccarelli Institute in Heliopolis amidst the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on July 8, 2020 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images hide caption

Move over, violins and pianos. The Seattle Symphony is giving the timpani its moment in the spotlight with a world premiere concerto. Principal timpanist Eric Schweikert, who says he is drawn to the back-of-the-classroom vibe in the orchestra, is stepping up to showcase the versatility of the percussion instrument. The piece offers listeners a look at the timpani's range, including rumbling rolls produced with clever mallet work to imitate the effect of a long note. While Schweikert promises to deliver plenty of the wild, Muppets-style Animal energy audiences crave, he's also ready to keep his fellow musicians on their toes — and show the crowd that kettle drums can sing, too.
Holiday travel can be stressful. Make a plan for potential flight disruptions with these tips. Aleksei Morozov/Getty Images hide caption

articles.title: The human cost of the electric vehicle boom is at the center of a lawsuit in Congo
paragraphs: A neighborhood on the outskirts of Kolwezi, Democratic Republic of Congo, where industrial mines encroach on homes and open-pit operations increasingly consume residential areas, Sept. 27. Marie Ruwet/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.
She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.
She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.

Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.

Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.
"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."
The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.

articles.title: Meet Colombia's fuzzy 'water guardians'
paragraphs: Frailejons, Colombia's iconic high-altitude plants, help protect the páramos that supply much of the country's water. John Otis for NPR hide caption
MONGUÍ, Colombia — Moisés Moreno greets visitors at his greenhouse 10,000 feet high in the Andes Mountains. Underneath the plastic roof, he nurtures tiny seedlings that can grow to be 30-feet tall.
"Do you know anything about frailejons?" Moreno asks his visitors, who are mostly clueless.
Related to the sunflower, frailejons are the iconic flora of Colombia's high mountain wetlands, which are known as páramos, and are vital for the country's water supply.

The wooly fuzz on their leaves protect frailejons from the cold and absorb water from the cloud cover. This helps maintain moisture in the páramos, which are the source of major rivers, and much of Colombia's water.

But frailejons and the páramos where they grow face a growing array of threats, including farmers, cattle ranchers and coal miners who are gradually pushing higher into the Andes. In addition, climate change is warming the mountains, allowing invasive species to survive at higher altitudes and disrupt their fragile ecosystems.

A cow sits among frailejón plants in Colombia's Andean páramo, a fragile high-altitude ecosystem that supplies water to much of the country. Ranching and farming threaten the plants' survival. John Otis for NPR hide caption

Of the nearly 150 species of frailejons, two-thirds are at risk and 17 are endangered, says Mauricio Diazgranados, a Colombian expert on the plant who is chief science officer at the New York Botanical Garden.

articles.title: Fighting between Russia and Ukraine has expanded geographically, drawing concerns
paragraphs: In recent days, Ukraine has sunk a Russian warship docked in port in Libya, and Russian missiles have landed in Poland. The Kremlin has not commented on the missiles.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST: Depending on your point of view, Russia's war in Ukraine is either revving up or winding down.STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: This month, the Trump administration claimed it was making progress toward a negotiated peace. Also this month, the fighting has expanded geographically into Eastern Europe, Northern Europe, even the Mediterranean, as if it was a world war.MARTIN: Joining us to talk about both these dynamics is NPR's Charles Maynes from Moscow. Charles, good morning.CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: Morning, Michel.MARTIN: So Russia and Ukraine are both striking out far beyond their borders. How concerned should we be?MAYNES: You know, there have been long concerns that an incident along NATO's northeastern flank near a border in Russia could serve as a tripwire for turning the war in Ukraine into a wider conflict. But recent events have brought that back to our attention. Last week we saw three Russian cruise missiles land in southeastern Poland, and on Saturday, a sanctioned Russian cargo ship was hit by what is presumed to have been a Ukrainian drone in the Baltic Sea. But now we're also seeing action further afield. Ukraine destroyed a Russian naval warship docked in Libya in the Mediterranean. Russia has its own shadow role providing intel to Iran in its war with the U.S. And just this morning, South Korea said it scrambled jets to chase away Russian sorties operating near its airspace. So the spillover is real, and the map is wide.MARTIN: So what is being done to contain it?MAYNES: Well, you know, Russian President Vladimir Putin constantly dismisses this idea that he's seeking direct confrontation with NATO. He says it's absurd. But there have been a spate of recent incidents of bomb threats, cyberattacks, sabotage that some in Europe believe are the work of Russia's security services. Russia's goal, it seems, would be to tear at the alliance's core commitment to collective security - this idea that an attack on one is an attack on all - and it's divided NATO. How do you respond to acts that fall below this threshold of outright war? So for example, President Trump has dismissed incursions by Russia into NATO airspace as basically mistakes. Now, as to other areas where we've seen Ukraine launch attacks, like Libya or apparently the Baltic Sea, it seems to show that Ukraine is intent on striking symbols of Russian power anywhere, and that also makes some supporters of Kyiv nervous.MARTIN: On the diplomatic front, President Trump is suggesting that a peace deal may be in the offing. Why does he say that?MAYNES: Well, after two years, we saw the Trump administration really make no headway. They've changed tactics by expanding the talks beyond Russia and Ukraine to focus on European security as a whole. And the conversations are now fundamentally centered on what security guarantees are on offer to Ukraine, to Russia, and to Europe.
